#7691. Arkansas Bar Official Allegedly Transferred Points from Some Bar Examinees to Others

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From the Arkansas Supreme Court Thursday:

Evidence exists that Givens harvested points from a number of examinees' scores and then added them to other examinees' scores within the same test administration. Thus, she unilaterally elevated some examinees' scores to the minimum passing score of 270 or greater. Brech also identified at least one instance in which score alterations may have reduced an examinee's score-who otherwise would have passed-to a failing score. And in at least one instance, the individual who should have received the top score on the Arkansas Bar Examination had their score reduced thereby naming another examinee as the recipient of the highest score on the exam. If these allegations are true, these actions constitute an unprecedented breach of public trust.

An internal review by Robert Brech, Executive Director of the Supreme Court of Arkansas's Office of Professional Conduct and Programs, has uncovered extensive irregularities involving the Court's Office of Professional Programs and the administration of the Arkansas Bar Examination. The matter was turned over to state and federal authorities.

As of today, the Prosecuting Attorney's Office for the Sixth Judicial District filed formal criminal charges against Nancie Givens for 65 counts of tampering with a public record under Arkansas Code Annotated section 5-54-121 in connection with the alleged altering of numerous Arkansas Bar Examination scores and the deletion of files purportedly intended to conceal that misconduct. The charges followed a criminal investigation initiated in April 2026 by the Arkansas State Police and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. As always, all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law.

Moving forward, we are committed to holding those involved accountable, taking continued corrective oversight of the Arkansas Bar Examination, and determining the appropriate course of action.

In February 2026, Givens, the former Executive Director of this Court's Office of Professional Programs, resigned. At that time, Robert Brech was serving as Executive Director of the Court's Office of Professional Conduct. Following Givens's resignation, the Court directed Brech to supervise the Office of Professional Programs, which oversees the administration of the Arkansas Bar Examination.

Upon his review of the Office of Professional Programs' records and administrative operations, Brech discovered that a large number of files and electronic communications were modified or deleted in early January 2026. Approximately 11,400 files were deleted or rendered unavailable. Most of those files included Arkansas Bar examinee applications, profiles, and examination score sheets that the Office of Professional Programs was required by this Court's rules to retain for twenty-five years.

Brech immediately notified a member of this Court, who directed him to determine the extent of the missing records and identify any other irregularities. On the basis of his review of the remaining files, Brech identified numerous discrepancies involving Arkansas Bar Examination scores across at least eight test administrations between July 2020 and July 2025. At that time, the matter was referred to the appropriate state and federal authorities.

Evidence exists that Givens harvested points from a number of examinees' scores and then added them to other examinees' scores within the same test administration. Thus, she unilaterally elevated some examinees' scores to the minimum passing score of 270 or greater. Brech also identified at least one instance in which score alterations may have reduced an examinee's score-who otherwise would have passed-to a failing score. And in at least one instance, the individual who should have received the top score on the Arkansas Bar Examination had their score reduced thereby naming another examinee as the recipient of the highest score on the exam. If these allegations are true, these actions constitute an unprecedented breach of public trust.

The vast majority of examinees who were previously informed that they had passed the Arkansas Bar Examination by the Office of Professional Programs did, in fact, pass the exam. Those examinees affected will be notified by the Office of Professional Conduct as soon as possible upon definitive confirmation of their status.

The Court is working with state and federal authorities to recover deleted and missing data, analyze all test administrations within that time frame, and determine the full scope of this grave and potentially criminal abuse of power. The people of Arkansas deserve, and the Court is committed to providing, total transparency in this matter. However, further disclosure will be forthcoming in a manner so as to not compromise the ongoing state and federal criminal investigations. Accordingly, additional disclosures will be limited as those efforts remain underway.

As an immediate step, independent of any state or federal criminal investigation or prosecution, Nancie Givens has been referred to the Office of Professional Conduct for investigation of extensive violations of the Arkansas Rules of Professional Conduct. See Ark. R. Prof. Conduct 8.1(a) & 8.4(a)-(e). Furthermore, new testing procedures and security measures were implemented with the February 2026 administration of the Arkansas Bar Examination to ensure systemic accountability and safeguard the integrity of the examination.

We recognize the profound consequences for affected examinees, the Bar, and the public at large. Our paramount concern is safeguarding litigants, the integrity of the legal profession, and public confidence in the administration of justice. While these matters remain under criminal and administrative investigation, we commit to pursue continued corrective measures in an effort to reestablish confidence in our institution.

#7690. Prosecution Over Threat to American Federation of Teachers President Randi Weingarten Can Go Forward

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From U.S. v. Spitzer (N.D. Ga.), filed by Magistrate Judge John Larkins on Oct. 9, and just affirmed Wednesday by Judge Eleanor Ross:

The indictment alleges that on July 23, 2024, Mr. Spitzer posted the following message on the website for the American Federation of Teachers, a labor union, regarding its president ("Individual #1"):

[Individual #1] is an ignorant incompetent cunt that should be worried for her safety. Fact that she is still alive. Liberal nazi deserves the bullet to head. Resign before she ends like what happened to trump at his speech. They won't miss fat bitch.

The indictment alleges that the post violated 18 U.S.C. § 875(c), which makes it a federal crime to transmit in interstate commerce any communication containing a threat to injure another person.

Mr. Spitzer argues that assuming the allegations in the indictment were true, it fails to state an offense because the posting was not a "true threat," or even a threat at all, and thus is protected by the First Amendment. As he sees it, the posting was simply political speech about a public figure and did not advocate the use of force or violence against Individual #1.

{In an effort to contextualize the posting, Mr. Spitzer points to an internet article in which Mike Pompeo, the former U.S. Secretary of State, described Individual #1 as "the most dangerous person in the world"; examples of "conservative politicians and commentators" criticizing her approach to school closures during the pandemic; and examples of Individual #1's own political statements. But these are not facts that the Court can consider at this juncture because they fall outside the four corners of the indictment.}

The government responds that whether Mr. Spitzer's posting qualified as a true threat is a question for the jury and that a pretrial determination of the sufficiency of the evidence is procedurally improper. The government further asserts that Mr. Spitzer improperly relies on facts not alleged in the indictment to contextualize the posting. The government has the better argument….

Considering the allegations on the face of the indictment—as this Court must—the Court finds that a jury could conclude that Mr. Spitzer's alleged posting constituted a "true threat." There are at least four separate references to harming or killing Individual #1, including: that she should be "worried for her safety"; that she "deserves a bullet to [the] head"; that unless she resigns she risks being shot similar to the attempted assassination of President Donald J. Trump; and that she will not be missed. In addition, the posting makes an oblique reference to her still being alive, which when combined with the other statements, can reasonably be interpreted as evidencing a present intent to intimidate and place Individual #1 in fear of bodily harm or death. The screed's liberal use of epithets further tends to show that the posting was not simply on a matter of public concern, but rather a threat against Individual #1 personally….

In his reply, Mr. Spitzer relies on the Supreme Court's decision in Watts v. United States, to argue that "political hyperbole" is not a "true threat." True enough, but Watts is distinguishable. In that case, the Supreme Court overturned the conviction of Watts, an 18-year-old Black protester who was charged with threatening President Lyndon B. Johnson during a political rally at the Washington Monument during the 1960's. During the protest, Watts said:

They always holler at us to get an education. And now I have already received my draft classification as 1-A and I have got to report for my physical this Monday coming. I am not going. If they ever make me carry a rifle the first man I want to get in my sights is L.B.J. They are not going to make me kill my black brothers.

The Supreme Court held that considering the full context of the statement—including that it was conditional upon Watt's joining the military (which he said he would not do) and that the listeners laughed at his statement—it was "political hyperbole," not a true threat. In contrast, Mr. Spitzer's alleged statement is much more threatening for the reasons explained above. Also, significantly, Watts was decided after trial, based on a developed evidentiary record, which underscores why dismissal at this juncture is not appropriate.

Accordingly, dismissal of the indictment is not warranted. But, of course, Mr. Spitzer is free to renew his challenge to the sufficiency of the evidence at trial….

Brent A. Gray and Eric John White represent the government.

#7689. Kim Kardashian aims to retake bar exam

Reality TV star Kim Kardashian speaks onstage during the 2020 Winter TCA Tour on Jan. 18, 2020, in Pasadena, California. (Photo by David Livingston/Getty Images)

Reality TV star Kim Kardashian still holds ambitions to become a lawyer and plans to retake the bar exam—someday.

Kardashian, who failed the California bar exam in 2025, said she is “always thinking about the bar” and is “still all in,” she told People on Monday. “I’m going to take my time and wait until the moment is right, when I have some free time to focus on it.”

Kardashian, who plays a lawyer on Hulu’s legal drama All’s Fair, was among the 7,362 candidates who completed the July 2025 administration of the California bar, according to the State Bar of California.

Kardashian did not attend law school and does not have an undergraduate degree. She has followed the state’s alternative pathway that allows candidates to take the bar exam by learning the law through apprenticeship and study.

California is one of the few states that allow lawyers to become lawyers by “reading the law.”

#7688. Court Allows Discovery as to Vindictive Prosecution Defense by Smartmatic's Parent Company

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

"It may well be that no fire will be discovered under all the smoke, but there is enough smoke here ... to warrant the unusual step of ... find[ing] out how this unusual prosecution came about."

From U.S. v. SGO Corp. Ltd., decided Tuesday by Judge Kathleen Williams (S.D. Fla.):

For a six-year period, the Government investigated SGO executives for their role in a money laundering and bribery scheme related to the May, 2016 Philippine elections. The investigation culminated in a six-count indictment ("First Indictment"), returned on August 8, 2024, which charged [executives of] SGO and Smartmatic … [with] conspiracy to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act ("FCPA") (Count I); violations of the FCPA (Count II); conspiracy to commit money laundering (Count III); and international laundering of monetary instruments (Counts IV, V, and VI). The FCPA "prohibits officers of a domestic concern from making corrupt payments to a 'foreign official.'"

SGO was not charged. In fact, SGO had been cooperating with the Government since 2021, years before the First Indictment was returned. {Although the Parties may dispute the breadth and quality of SGO's efforts to cooperate, there is no question that SGO and the Government were engaged in discussions and the exchange of documents related to this matter.}

The original trial date was set for October 7, 2024 … [but was eventually reset for 2026]….

As the court notes, the Trump Administration was skeptical of FCPA prosecutions, deprioritized FCPA enforcement generally, and "elected to close FCPA investigations into multiple companies." But despite that, in October 2025, the government added SGO as a defendant in the case. SGO then moved to dismiss the superseding indictment, alleging vindictive and selective prosecution, and sought discovery in support of that motion, "premised on political events that have embroiled Smartmatic in the wake of the 2020 election":

Since that election, multiple high-profile individuals and organizations connected to then-Former President Donald Trump have alleged that Smartmatic, a subsidiary of SGO, interfered in the election…. President Trump has also reposted content blaming Smartmatic for interfering in United States and Venezuelan elections, calling Smartmatic "disgraceful" and expressing that those who "rigged" the 2020 election must pay. In response to the statements by President Trump's confederates, Smartmatic brought various defamation suits, which are largely ongoing. SGO contends that President Trump's personal animus against SGO and assertion of its rights against President Trump's confederates precipitated the filing of the Superseding Indictment….

The court lays out the demanding standard for defendants' attempts to get discovery related to allegations of vindictive or selective prosecution, but concludes that in this case the standard was met. A brief excerpt (for more, including citations to precedents to which the court analogizes this case, see the full opinion):

First, a vindictive prosecution claim may be supported by evidence that the Government bucked a trend in enforcement activity in prosecuting the defendant…. [W]hile the Blanche and Bondi Memos and Executive Order 14209 explicitly announced an intention to rein in and limit FCPA enforcement, particularly against corporations, SGO was charged, nonetheless.

Second, a vindictive prosecution claim may be supported by the timing between a defendant's assertion of a right and the allegedly vindictive prosecutorial act…. [Here,] it is telling that the Government chose not to indict SGO originally, that SGO was charged only after President Trump reassumed office and after SGO had been cooperating with the Government for years, and that the Government has presented no evidence adduced between the First and Superseding Indictments warranting SGO's addition as a defendant.

Third, a vindictive prosecution claim may be supported by the Executive, prosecutor, or law enforcement's stated positions, even when they do not explicitly admit that the case was brought against the defendant for an improper purpose…. The Court finds probative not just that President Trump signed an executive order regarding FCPA enforcement but also that President Trump has personally expressed animus towards SGO regarding election interference. Indeed, President Trump's confederates were sued by SGO for making false claims regarding SGO's role in interfering with the 2020 presidential election that President Trump lost….

After evaluating the totality of the circumstances in this case, the Court has concluded that limited discovery regarding SGO's Motion to Dismiss is warranted…. [T]ere is "some evidence" tending to support SGO's Motion to Dismiss: the individual Defendants were charged over a year prior to when the Superseding Indictment against SGO was returned; for years prior to the initiation of this case and up until the Superseding Indictment was returned, SGO was cooperating with the Government; the Government charged SGO amidst a public shift away from charging defendants for similar FCPA violations; SGO brought suit against the President's confederates prior to being charged; and the President has expressed at least some degree of animus towards SGO. "It may well be that no fire will be discovered under all the smoke, but there is enough smoke here … to warrant the unusual step of … find[ing] out how this unusual prosecution came about."

[T]he Government shall provide the Court with the following for ex parte and in camera review under seal:

#7686. Wells Fargo faces labor board complaint over union vote

The National Labor Relations Board alleged the lender threatened and retaliated against workers in favor of unionization at a California branch.

The National Labor Relations Board has accused Wells Fargo of illegally threatening and retaliating against employees and coercing workers to prevent fair unionization votes at a California branch.

Most employees of an Atwater, California, branch who signed cards supporting unionization in December 2023 voted against unionization the following month, a regional director of the NLRB alleged, in a complaint filed Feb. 11 and seen by Bloomberg,

The NLRB claims Wells Fargo coerced workers to vote against unionization. Wells Fargo has denied that allegation.

The labor board wants the bank to recognize and negotiate with the union despite the vote, based on a 2023 precedent case. The 2023 Cemex ruling strengthened the NLRB's power to compel companies that violate labor laws to recognize unions.

However, Republicans and business groups oppose the precedent. The acting general counsel of NLRB, William Cowen, or his permanent replacement, could withdraw, amend, or settle the Wells Fargo complaint.

President Donald Trump appointed Cowen acting general counsel this month, days after firing NLRB’s previous chief lawyer Jennifer Abruzzo, a Biden appointee, and Democratic board member Gwynne Wilcox.

The email notifying Wilcox of her termination said she was being fired since she did not “share the objectives” of the present administration. Wilcox’s ouster has left the board with only two members coupled with existing vacancies and does not meet the minimum number of members needed to adjudicate routine cases.

Wilcox is suing Trump, alleging the president surpassed his authority in firing her and requesting that she be allowed to resume her work as an NLRB member.

The NLRB complaint does not signify a complete investigation or a full adjudication of the allegations; rather, the regional office found that the allegations may be sufficient to go to a hearing to consider all evidence and make credibility determinations, a Wells Fargo spokesperson noted.

Employees at the Atwater branch voted 3-1 to reject unionization in January 2024. The branch manager allegedly told staff she knew about organizing discussions and warned about camera surveillance. She also reportedly told workers that Wells Fargo would apply stricter work conditions and would make union supporters stay longer hours.

A Wells Fargo spokesperson said the bank trains its managers to respect the rights of its employees to freely associate and join or support a union, or to bargain collectively with a representative of their choosing.

“We train our managers to comply with labor law and respect the rights of our employees,” the spokesperson told Banking Dive via email. “In this case, the majority of eligible employees freely voted against a union in a Board supervised secret ballot election and the facts do not support allegations to the contrary.”

Wells Fargo is cooperating with the investigation but believes these allegations are unfounded and plans to defend the company and employees, the spokesperson added.

An NLRB hearing before a judge is scheduled for October, and Wells Fargo, if ordered to collectively bargain, can appeal to NLRB members in Washington, Bloomberg reported.

Recently, unionized Wells Fargo employees hit a new challenge in organizing. The bank's conduct management intake team won its union vote 21-16 in December, making it the first non-branch unit at Wells Fargo to unionize.

The team, which handles customer and employee complaints across various locations, has now filed an unfair labor practice charge with the NLRB through Wells Fargo Workers United-CWA. The complaint alleges that the bank illegally refuses to engage in collective bargaining following the certified union vote, American Banker reported. However, the bank contends it’s waiting for the outcome of the NLRB’s review and claims there were procedural flaws in the handling of the vote.

CWA unionized 24 Wells Fargo branches last year, with around 200 employees being organized.

Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf pushed back on employee unionization efforts last April, saying it’s important to “make clear that we continue to believe that our employees are best served by working directly with Wells Fargo and our leadership team.”

Judiciary efforts to create rules for artificial intelligence use in the courts have been stalled amid concerns over the feasibility of reaching consensus on how the issues should be handled. (Photo by imaginima/Getty Images)

Judiciary efforts to create rules for artificial intelligence use in the courts have been stalled amid concerns over the feasibility of reaching consensus on how the issues should be handled.

The Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules, which advises the Judicial Conference of the United States, has been developing rules for AI use for several years, but efforts have encountered setbacks and resistance, slowing down the possibility of any new policy.

Attorneys, scholars and judges have criticized proposed evidentiary rules, such as one involving how to handle AI deepfakes, according to a story by Law360.

“Bottom line: I’m not hopeful at this point,” Maura R. Grossman, a professor at the University of Waterloo in Canada whose research has shaped the AI proposals, told Law360.

#7683. Impeach Pete Hegseth

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

He deserves it for his role in starting an unconstitutional war and perpetrating over 200 murders.

Outgoing GOP Representative Thomas Massie is planning to introduce an impeachment resolution against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. Soon-to-be Democratic Speaker of the House Hakeem Jeffries says he's a "hard yes" on the idea. That makes it very likely it will happen. If not now, then when Democrats take control of Congress in January, after their big win in the midterm election. Hegseth richly deserves it, and should be convicted on at least two major charges: his role in starting an unconstitutional war and over 200 cases of outright murder.

On September 15, Rep. Massie outlined eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth (see here for his more detailed description). The two most compelling are these:

Article I - Waging War in Contravention of the War Powers Resolution of 1973 Section 2(c): Charges Secretary Hegseth with waging the Iran war despite no declaration of war, statutory authorization, attack on the United States, or imminent threat. It establishes that the war was unlawful from its inception….

Article V - Extrajudicial Killings: Charges Secretary Hegseth with replacing maritime law enforcement with unauthorized lethal military targeting of suspected drug traffickers, resulting in at least 221 deaths. It also addresses denial of quarter, secondary strikes on survivors, failure to rescue shipwrecked persons, and the creation of artificial legal authorities for the campaign.

Massie's Article V is the single most damning, in my view. Hegseth is a principal architect of the Trump Administration's campaign of "drug boat" strikes in the Caribbean and the Pacific. It has now killed an estimated 244 people, virtually all of them civilians (Massie's September figure of 221 is now somewhat outdated).

I have previously written about why these strikes are illegal (see here and here). But don't take my word for it, or even that of other libertarian or left-liberal experts, like Brian Finucane. Take that of John Yoo, former Bush Administration official, and leading academic advocate of sweeping executive power over foreign policy and national security issues. If you illegally order the deliberate killing of civilians - especially outside the context of a war - that's outright murder. And that's exactly what Pete Hegseth has done.

This would be true even if those killed were all would-be drug dealers seeking to transport illegal drugs for sale in the US. I have previously explained why it is unjust and illegal to kill suspected drug dealers out of hand and why they are not the legal or moral equivalent of terrorists or enemy combatants in a war. As GOP Sen. Rand Paul pointed out when the drug boat strikes began, "The reason we have trials and we don't automatically assume guilt is what if we make a mistake and they happen to be people fleeing the Venezuelan dictator? … off our coast it isn't our policy just to blow people up … even the worst people in our country, they still get a trial." But, in fact, the evidence indicates most were not on their way to the US and many were not transporting drugs at all. Some, for example, were just fishermen.

The Constitution allows impeachment and removal of executive branch officials for "high crimes and misdemeanors." You don't have to be a lawyer or legal scholar to figure out that complicity in over 200 murders qualifies as a "high crime."

Hegseth is also a key architect of the disastrous Iran War. In previous writings, I have explained why that war is illegal, violating both the Constitution, and the War Powers Act of 1973. Such a war requires congressional authorization, and Trump and Hegseth did not even try to get it. The war's illegality is one of the main reasons for its failure to this point, as failure to secure the broad public support needed to get congressional authorization  ensured Trump lacked staying power to continue the fight effectively after the initial strikes didn't achieve a quick, decisive victory.

Initiating and waging an illegal war isn't a violation of criminal law (though perhaps it should be). But massive non-criminal illegal acts and abuses of power are impeachable under the history and original meaning of the Impeachment Clause of the Constitution. On that point, see analyses by Gene Healy of the Reason Foundation (formerly at the Cato Institute), and prominent conservative legal scholars Michael Stokes Paulsen (here, here, and here), and Keith Whittington. There are few bigger illegal abuses of power than starting a massive unconstitutional war.

In fairness, Trump and Hegseth are not alone in starting illegal wars. Barack Obama did it, too, with his unconstitutional wars against Libya and ISIS (which, for those keeping score, I condemned at the time). Obama likely deserved to be impeached, as well. But the fact that he got away with this illegality is no reason to spare Hegseth. To the contrary, past laxness is all the more reason to reestablish deterrence to prevent future wrongdoing. Furthermore, Trump and Hegseth's illegal war is on a much larger scale than Obama's were, and has had far worse results.

The only potentially valid objection to impeaching Hegseth is that it might fail, and backfire politically. But the Iran War is highly unpopular, and therefore impeachment on that basis is unlikely to backfire. The politics of the boat strikes is more debatable. The administration will surely try to defend them by arguing the victims deserved it because they were trying to smuggle dangerous drugs. But that can be countered by presenting the extensive evidence demonstrating that many were not on their way to the US or even transporting drugs at all. Testimony from members of the bereaved families of the victims can help make that point, and influence public opinion against Hegseth and the administration.

Hegseth is unpopular on Capitol Hill, which makes it potentially possible to secure the needed 11 or more GOP senators' votes required for conviction (the Democrats are going to have 54-56 senators in the next Congress, depending on the results of still-ongoing vote counts in close races in Alaska and Mississippi). But even if he gets acquitted, the process of impeachment and trial can send a useful signal, and further publicize the administration's massive criminality and wrongdoing.

Obviously, the ultimate perpetrator of these illegal acts is not Hegseth, but Trump. The former was following the latter's illegal orders (though he likely also helped influence Trump to give those orders in the first place). But sanctioning officials for obeying illegal orders is still important. That's one of the lessons of the Nuremberg trials. And, hopefully, the time will come for Trump to face sanctions for his many illegal actions, as well. As with Hegseth, the only plausible argument against impeaching him is political, not legal or moral.

Massie's impeachment resolution also outlines several other charges against Hegseth. I think most of them have merit, but are less significant than those covered above. I will not attempt to assess these other charges here.

UPDATE: Back in 2020, I critiqued the "slippery slope" argument against impeaching presidents for abuses of power that aren't technically crimes. My points apply with even greater force to any such argument against impeaching appointed officials, like Hegseth. In their case, there is no argument they have some kind of popular mandate from the electorate.

#7682. Second Amendment Roundup: Viramontes Is Not Moot

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Cook County includes AK-47 rifles to be among “AR-15 platform weapons”

In the Viramontes v. Cook County case pending in the Supreme Court, Cook County has filed a Suggestion of Mootness in response to a Motion to Dismiss Petitioner Cutberto Viramontes from the case.  The question presented in the case is: "Whether the Second and Fourteenth Amendments guarantee the right to possess AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles."  Cook County argues that standing in the challenge is based on Mr. Viramontes' wish to obtain an AR-15 style rifle, but Christopher Khaya, the only other individual petitioner in the case, only wishes to obtain an AK-47 style rifle.  Mr. Khaya, the argument goes, does not have standing to litigate the question presented because he did not state he wishes to obtain an AR-15.

Yet Cook County itself previously classified the AK-47 as within the general category "AR-15 platform weapons."  The Brief for the Cook County Respondents states:

Specific firearms are outlawed under the Ordinance, including the "AK-47," "AR-15," "Bushmaster XM15," "Bushmaster Carbon 15," "Bushmaster MOE series," "ArmaLite M15," "Armalite M15-T," and "Olympic Arms PCR." [Cook County, Ill., Code of Ordinances] § 54-211(7) (hereafter AR-15 platform weapons).

The County uses the term "AR-15 platform weapons" throughout its Brief as a convenient shorthand to describe the types of rifles it bans.  For instance, referring to how "the public increasingly purchased AR-15 platform weapons," in the next sentence it describes a shooting in which the perpetrator used "a semiautomatic AK-47 style rifle."  Describing the features that tie such rifles together, the Brief states: "The Ordinance is limited to 'assault weapons' that are strictly defined as 'semiautomatic rifle[s]' able to accept a detachable large capacity magazine and one or more of certain military-style features, such as a folding or telescoping stock, a pistol grip without a stock, a barrel shroud, or a muzzle brake."  (There is actually nothing specifically "military-style" about such features.)

In its Suggestion of Mootness, the County attempts to separate these common features by distinguishing the different model names and designs.  Viramontes sought "to own a Smith and Wesson Military & Police AR-15 style semiautomatic rifle," while Khaya "wants an IMI [Industrial Military Industries] Galil semiautomatic rifle," which the petitioners themselves stated "is not an AR-15 style rifle but is largely based on the AK-47 design."  But the question presented is not that narrow, instead referring generally to "AR-15 platform and similar semiautomatic rifles."  To that, the County claims: "There are no record facts concerning whether the IMI Galil weapon operates similarly to an AR-15."  For starters, how about the County's own Brief describing their common features to be that they are semiautomatic rifles, have the ability to accept a detachable magazine, and have a pistol grip, folding or telescoping stock, and a muzzle brake?

In sum, in its Brief, Cook County refers to "AK-47" rifles as encompassed in the general term "AR-15 platform weapons."  Its denial of that in its Suggestion of Mootness cannot be regarded as well taken.  Mr. Khaya has standing to litigate the question presented.  There are also two association challengers who thereby also have standing.

In any event, as Cook County notes in its filing, Viramontes is consolidated with Grant v. Higgins, the challenge to Connecticut's prohibition on semiautomatic rifles, which is quite similar to that of Cook County. Therefore, regardless of what happens with Cook County's suggestion of mootness, the Grant case will be unaffected, and the Supreme Court is poised to decide this fundamental issue that lays at the heart of the Second Amendment.

Stephen Halbrook is a Senior Fellow with the Independent Institute. His latest books are America's Rifle: The Case for the AR-15 and The Right to Bear Arms: A Constitutional Right of the People or a Privilege of the Ruling Class? He is also author of The Founders' Second Amendment, Securing Civil Rights, Gun Control in the Third Reich, and Gun Control in Nazi-Occupied France. He has written over 30 law review articles and has testified in Congressional hearings on firearm law bills. He has also litigated extensively in the field, often representing groups such as the NRA, National African American Gun Association, Western States Sheriffs' Association, Congress of Racial Equality, National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers, and more. He has argued before the U.S. Supreme Court in Castillo v. U.S. (2000), Printz v. U.S. (1997), and U.S. v. Thompson/Center Arms Co. (1992), as well as in front of many other courts.  In D.C. v. Heller, he filed an amici curiae brief on behalf of a majority of members of Congress.

#7681. Lawyers’ AI use doesn’t justify slashing $115K fee award, appellate court says

A federal appeals court has rejected an argument that a law firm’s use of artificial intelligence should shrink its fee award. (Image from Shutterstock)

A federal appeals court has rejected an argument that a law firm’s use of artificial intelligence should shrink its fee award.

Reuters reported Monday that the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Denver upheld a $115,000 fee awarded to defense lawyers at Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck by the lower court in a trade secrets dispute. The trial court had ruled that the fee was reasonable.

“Plaintiffs have not shown that defense counsel’s use of AI rendered the hours that ​they actually expended unreasonable,” wrote 10th Circuit Judge Carolyn McHugh for a unanimous three-judge panel.

The appeals court also upheld the ​dismissal of the lawsuit.

In her opinion, McHugh acknowledged that AI and similar research tools can make attorneys more efficient. But she stressed that lawyers must still verify legal authorities and arguments themselves.

According to Reuters, the case began in 2024, when industrial motor-efficiency equipment maker Flux Drive filed a suit against a Chinese manufacturer, alleging that one of its former engineers had stolen proprietary information and given it to them. After the case was dismissed, Flux Drive was ordered to pay the defendants’ legal fees. On appeal, the company argued that the defense billed for “ministerial tasks,” and that AI use should have lowered the bill.

The defendants countered that their lawyers checked every piece of AI-assisted research, and that Flux Drive pointed to no specific inflated entry, redundant task or unreasonable charge.

Brownstein Hyatt partner Christopher Ottele, who represented the defendants, called AI a powerful tool that sophisticated firms should embrace.

“This ​decision confirms that the use of AI is not a substitute for the judgment and analysis that attorneys still ​must exercise in every filing with the court,” Ottele told Reuters.

Counsel for the plaintiffs did not immediately respond to Reuters’ requests for comment.

#7680. Talarico's Christianity

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Christian nationalism is bad but Christian socialism is good.

The media continues to fawn over Texas's new Senator-Elect, James Talarico. The New York Times draws a contrast between the traditional conservative evangelicalism and Talarico's progressive christianity.

Mr. Talarico, an eighth-generation Texan and onetime seminarian, understood all that. His own grandfather, once a Baptist preacher, found himself on the "moderate" side when conservatives took over the Southern Baptist Convention in the 1970s and '80s, a move masterminded in Texas. Mr. Talarico was raised in a church that has been known locally for its progressive activism for decades.

In a town hall hosted by CNN in October, a voter from his hometown of Round Rock, Texas, pressed him "Christian to Christian" about provocative past statements like "God is nonbinary."

"Do you believe that the Bible is the absolute source of truth and God's final authoritative word, even when our culture says otherwise?" she asked.

For many, his rise was a reminder of the capacious borders of Christianity in the state.

"The loudest voices that people hear are these megachurches, and they think that's what we're all doing," said the Rev. Janet Maykus. She was raised in a progressive church in then-rural Lancaster, Texas, where she was taught that "faith is something particular to every person," rooted in justice and kindness rather than doctrine.

Ms. Maykus, 64, now leads the United Christian Church of Austin, a small mainline Protestant congregation in the capital.

When her congregation recites the Lord's Prayer, it's a "train wreck," she said fondly. Some people recite a version with gender-inclusive language; others tack on a few extra words here and there. In every service, Ms. Maykus also prays aloud for "our siblings in Christ who have lost their way to the lure of white Christian nationalism."

In recent months, she said, she has talked with multiple visitors to the church who said they had been inspired by Mr. Talarico to seek out a church like hers. She is baptizing a baby on Sunday.

The growth of progressive congregations like hers is exactly why Robert Jeffress, pastor of the politically influential church First Baptist Dallas, watched Mr. Talarico's ascent with alarm, he said in an interview this week.

"What James Talarico believes about the Bible and about Jesus, those beliefs don't disqualify him from being a senator, but they do disqualify him from being a Christian pastor, or even a Christian," Mr. Jeffress said, referring in part to Mr. Talarico's suggestion that Christianity is not the only religion that points to the truth.

Last Sunday, Mr. Jeffress said, he alluded to Mr. Talarico as he preached about the tower of Babel, warning how "false religion always mixes truth with error."

Mr. Jeffress's church, established in the 1860s, is one of many institutions that have long made Texas a major exporter of politically conservative Christianity.

Texas is where the folksy fundamentalist radio host W. Lee O'Daniel became governor in 1938, with a platform based on the Ten Commandments and low taxes. It's where W.A. Criswell, a predecessor of Mr. Jeffress, called the separation of church and state "the figment of some infidel's imagination" in 1984. And it's where Dan Patrick, the state's current lieutenant governor, described his socially conservative agenda as an expression of his Christian faith.

I have gotten into trouble in the past for writing about progressive Jewish faiths. I suppose I will do the same with progressive Christian faiths.

Is there any facet of Talarico's progressive political views that depart from Talarico's Christian beliefs? Stated differently, is Talarico's Christian beliefs merely an extension of Talarico's progressive political views? We are often told that conservative Christians distort scripture to support their policy preferences. Do progressive Christians also distort scripture to support their policy preferences?

When conservative Christians find support for their political beliefs in their faith, they are described as Christian Nationalists. What is the comparable label for progressive Christians who find support for their political beliefs in their faith? Perhaps it should be called Christian Socialism?

I think the same rule ought to apply to people of faith on all sides of the spectrum.

#7679. S.J. Bennett on the brilliance of 1960s British mysteries and thrillers

My first date with my husband, twenty-five years ago, was a series of tests. Do you like Blackadder, and agree that series 4 is the best? Are you a fan of Bladerunner? The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy? And, very importantly, did you read Len Deighton as a teenager? Luckily for our future son, we both passed.

Deighton’s unpredictable protagonists, and his propulsive writing style, were a revelation to sixteen year-old me. I always think of his heroes in cars, on the run from something awful, on the way to something worse.

Growing up in the 80s, I was a fan of the classics, of P.G. Wodehouse and Jilly Cooper. People behaved badly, very badly sometimes, but their role in the moral universe was clear. Then, in books written at around the time I was born, as the dust was finally settling from WW II, I found myself in the cynical, murky world of double agents and double-crossing, inspired in part by the Noir of the 30s, but updated to the Cold War: we can’t trust the men in charge, and the world may be about to end.

In the historical series that I’m writing featuring the late Queen, I’ve reached the mid-60s. The last book was set at the height of the space race in 1961, and the new one takes place in the Caribbean in 1966. I think of this as a sunny highlight: the Swinging Sixties, The Beatles, Carnaby Street, the young Rolling Stones….

But research quickly reminded me that it was the time of Vietnam, the Bay of Pigs, the call for independence among many of the UK’s old colonies, of drugs and disillusion, fear and paranoia. This is the world that Deighton explored in Funeral in Berlin.

His unnamed protagonist, played by Michael Caine and given the name Harry Palmer in the films (because it was the most boring one they could jointly come up with), had already had two outings, in The IPCRESS File and Horse Under Water. Both are a bit bonkers. Funeral in Berlin, published in 1964, was where Deighton really got into his stride.

The Berlin Wall had only gone up three years before. I lived there in the 80s, when the Wall went round the back of our garden and there was a Russian sentry post a few meters beyond. People were still dying in the attempt to get across, but by then, the Wall had its own mythology.

When Deighton was writing, the weird cruelty of streets and even houses being cut in half by barbed wire and concrete was still fresh, and bled into the text. I equally loved John Le Carré for his more cerebral evocation of the times, but Deighton’s working-class anti-hero, at odds with the Establishment and unwilling to look away, was the one who really got me into the genre.

How does Frederick Forsyth get away with the plot of The Day of the Jackal? Set in 1962, in the aftermath of the Algerian war of independence, it’s a story in which we already know the outcome—the assassin must surely fail to kill Charles de Gaulle, who didn’t die until 1970—and yet we’re gripped as we watch him regularly outwit the authorities, who are no slouches in tracking him down.

Inserting a false narrative into real events is what I do with my own series, so I’m with him as Forsyth tightly interweaves the two. I always used to feel that the final-final twist, where a character we think is dead shows up unexpectedly, didn’t quite make sense. However, when I recently relistened to the audiobook version, I realized that it had been set up that way all along. It makes the reader completely rethink the middle section, paying tribute to the value of dogged police work, even when the odds against success seem overwhelming.

The novel also pits a middle-class hero, the police deputy commissioner Claude Lebel, against a dismissive, upper-class superior. The moment when Lebel gets his revenge is very satisfying. Like Deighton, Forsyth was no fan of the old-school ruling classes, although he had an obvious respect for methodical assassins.

James Bond (another iconic spy name designed to be as boring as possible) evolved gradually as a character. He was based in part on old Etonian Ian Fleming himself, partly on some of the men he encountered in wartime naval intelligence, and later on the director of Dr No on screen, the refined and sophisticated Terence Young, It was Young who gave him his sharp tailoring from Anthony Sinclair, his taste for martinis and elegant way with cigarettes.

But the first man to play him, with a panther-like grace that got him the part, grew up in a tenement in Edinburgh, leaving home to work as a bricklayer, lorry driver and coffin polisher, among other things. Would Bond have been as interesting if he hadn’t had the magnetism that Sean Connery brought to the role? At a time of great social mobility, he was a stand-out star.

Connery didn’t play Bond in the film of On Her Majesty’s Secret Service. By 1969, he’d given up on the carnival of publicity around his life. But he was filming Dr No near Fleming’s Goldeneye estate in 1962 when Fleming wrote the novel.

Fleming probably had Connery (and those Anthony Sinclair suits) in mind for the Bond who pretends to be Sir Hilary Bray from the London College of Arms. In the end, though, the part went to the actor George Lazenby, who made the somewhat premature decision that James Bond would be a busted flush in the 1970s, and turned down a chance to return.

In this book, Blofeld is the villain, and the plot moves on from classic Cold War territory to a more generalized tech-driven anxiety, in which a bio-war is about to be unleashed by unsuspecting female debutantes. It’s not the most feminist of plots, but I love the novel for Bond’s female companion, Tracy di Vicenzo, the only woman in the Bond canon—apart from Vesper Lynd—who I think holds her own in a three-dimensional way.

Played to perfection by Diana Rigg onscreen, Tracy is smart, well-connected (her father is a very serious crime boss), reckless, resourceful, quick-thinking and athletic. Having created a woman who’s a worthy match for Bond, the series obviously couldn’t keep her. The ending of is so tragic and unexpected that it’s still gut-wrenching, even now.

On the whole, I’d say we don’t think of Agatha Christie when we think of the 1960s. The perennial films and TV series conjure inter-war fashions, Miss Marple’s Edwardian correctness, old-fashioned country houses, and the Art Deco smartness of Hercule Poirot.

But her success spanned decades. The Pale Horse, published in 1961, was partly inspired by the very popular novels by Dennis Wheatley, which often featured the supernatural. In Christie’s version we have foggy nights, witches, deserted country lanes and several predicted deaths in seemingly-impossible circumstances.

One of the secrets of Christie’s success was how cutting-edge she was with her murder methods. She loved to know about new poisons and the latest gadgets. Think of the role a Dictaphone plays in one of her most famous early books—Dictaphone as a company had only been created three years before it was published in the 1920s.

And true to the Christie formula, the solution to the Pale Horse mystery contains an up-to-date knowledge of chemistry. It works both as an out-of-time, spooky novel and a contemporary, 1960s plot.

In my books, Queen Elizabeth II occasionally has a Dick Francis novel at her bedside, and she was a big fan in real life. As a jockey, Francis was closely connected with the royal family. He was riding the Queen Mother’s horse, Devon Loch, towards victory in the 1956 Grand National, when the horse inexplicably fell. This was when he retired to become a writer.

Dead Cert, which came out in 1962, was his first novel. It’s centered around great horses falling in important races, and Francis’s visceral first-hand experience lights up the page. But there’s more to his books than horses. As Britain’s post-war economy took off, he branched out with his wife, Mary, to research a wide range of industries. exploring the glamour and danger of his age.

Like Deighton’s, I read his books in the 1980s, when Proof grabbed my attention. I’m drawn to Francis’s vulnerable heroes, so gentle with horses, so outrageously lucky or unlucky with women, so tough at withstanding injuries of all kinds (as the author was) and beatings from his sadistic villains. I have to read through half-closed eyelids, but still, I have to read on.

One of the things I like about Dick Francis’ career is that it took time to take off. Like Ian Fleming’s, his early books sold well enough, but there weren’t any fireworks. It was only as the series progressed that publicity grew, and he became the crimewriting juggernaut his estate still is today. There’s a lesson for publishers there, perhaps: have faith in your writers. Stick with them. Fandom comes with time and repetition.

It’s a lesson another British spy novelist embodies. Mick Herron’s Slough House books languished in the also-rans for years, until a US publisher spotted them and they got a new lease of life.

This autumn, season 6 of Slow Horses returns triumphantly to our screens. It contains many of the tropes of its 1960s predecessors: downtrodden heroes, defying the odds and besting upper class antagonists; realistically dingy streets and double-crossing; up-to-date technology and an overarching sense of anxiety. We can’t trust the men in charge, and the world may be about to end. Plus ça change.

SJ Bennett is the author of the international mystery series featuring Queen Elizabeth II as a secret solver of crimes. She has written over a dozen novels for both adults and children, and her award-winning books have been optioned for TV and translated into over 20 languages. She lives in London, where she writes in a shed at the bottom of her garden.

#7678. The SEC has requested to delay climate rule arguments. What’s next?

Sustainable investing experts are not surprised by the delay and say it is expected to have minimal immediate impact.

Acting Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Mark Uyeda’s decision last week to ask the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals to delay arguments for the agency’s climate risk disclosure rule did not come as a surprise to regulatory experts in the space.

While the change is expected to have minimal immediate impact, it sets the stage for a shift in focus for the SEC under the Trump administration.

The SEC issued its long-awaited climate-risk disclosure rule last March, nearly two years after it was first proposed — and amid over 24,000 public comments. Uyeda was one of two commissioners to vote against the rule’s approval. The rule was immediately met with multiple lawsuits that were later consolidated into the Eighth Circuit. The spate of legal challenges led the agency to stay the rule’s implementation in April.

Given the agency’s stay and the change in administration, Tom Willman, regulatory lead for artificial intelligence sustainability platform Clarity AI, said Uyeda’s decision came “as no great surprise.”

“It is nevertheless disappointing that investors will be deprived of much-needed financially material information related to climate related risks,” Willman said by email Wednesday.

Julie Gorte, senior vice president of sustainable investing at Impax Asset Management was more blunt in an interview: “The only person on the planet who didn't see this coming was Rip Van Winkle,” she said Wednesday.

Uyeda’s recommended pullback on defending the SEC climate rule follows his prior critiques of the rule. During the hearing on the final climate rule, in the weeks after it was finalized and in his Feb. 11 statement announcing the delay request, Uyeda maintained his belief that the SEC does not have the authority to promulgate the rule or require such disclosures.

Jenner & Block Partner Jennifer Lee, a former assistant director of the SEC Enforcement Division, said Uyeda’s position is “consistent with the new, Republican-led SEC’s shift back to focusing on ‘bread and butter’ investor disclosure issues.” Lee, who now represents companies and financial institutions in regulatory investigations and litigation, told ESG Dive in emailed comments Thursday that she expects that focus to include an emphasis on materiality, while looking to avoid “overly prescriptive disclosure requirements for public companies.”

The change in SEC posture, however, is expected to have a minimal impact for companies or investors, according to Willman and Gorte.

“The impact of this is going to be extraordinarily minimal, partly because it was never enforced in the first place,” Gorte said Wednesday. “So we never had better climate reporting stimulated by U.S. regulatory postures to begin with. And for U.S. companies, or for any company really, a lot of the big ones are probably still going to have to be reporting on all the same things that were in that rule because of [other jurisdictions].”

Willman echoed that note and said that many U.S. companies already voluntarily report climate risks due to investor demand, in addition to growing regulatory requirements both overseas in jurisdictions like the European Union, and stateside in California. New York recently reintroduced its own version of California’s climate disclosure laws.

Additionally, Stephen O’Day, a partner at Smith, Gambrell & Russell, noted the intervenors in the case could continue the rule’s defense, even though the SEC’s announcement indicates this iteration of the agency is not inclined to defend the rules. In the case of the climate rule, 18 states and the District of Columbia have signed on as intervenors to support the agency’s rule.

O’Day said a similar process happened after intervenors continued the defense for enforcement actions taken by the Clinton-era administration for violations of the Clean Air Act by coal-fired plants. Ultimately, the intervenors prevailed, and the Supreme Court upheld the actions.

“The proceedings pending in the Eighth Circuit involve challenges filed by multiple parties and intervenors, any of which could seek to continue defense of the SEC rules,” O’Day said. “So, while the court may grant the requested 45-day pause, it remains to be seen whether any such pause will result in the end of the SEC’s final rules.”

Regardless, sustainability programs and disclosures are expected to continue.

“Regulatory shifts don’t change the fundamental reality: physical climate risk is already priced into markets,” Lukky Ahmed, CEO of climate risk data and analytics platform Climate X, said by email Wednesday. Firms have a fiduciary responsibility to continue to assess, manage and disclose climate risks to their operations, Ahmed said.

“Integrating climate resilience and adaptation strategies isn’t just prudent — it’s essential for maintaining business performance, driving shareholder returns, and protecting communities," Ahmed said.

Despite the shifting federal policy stance, “there is a lot of faith that the drivers of sustainability remain in place no matter who is in anyone's White House,” Gorte told ESG Dive.

“If we don't solve the climate crisis, there are going to be … parts of the globe that are probably uninhabitable, or where people can't work outdoors in the summer. If we don't solve the biodiversity crisis, the prospects are even worse.” Gorte said. “So there are things that we have to do in order to preserve what we think of as life as we know it, and those drivers are going to remain in place.”

#7676. 7 essential 1970s NYC noir books and films

Noir fiction has been defined as a world of cynicism, fatalism, and moral ambiguity. Although it may have originated between the two World Wars in Dashiell Hammett’s San Francisco and Raymond Chandler’s Los Angeles, noir was reborn in the 1970’s of New York City. Each decade has its own quality, reflecting the social and political turmoil of its time, but the NYC 1970’s remains distinctive for the gritty style of the books and movies instilled from real life.

All of these stories have the personal struggles, the morally ambiguous decisions, and the political cynicism that form noir’s fatalism. Each novel ends with satisfying operatic tragedy, the dark and the light that coexists in the chiaroscuro world of noir. My teenage years spanned the 1970’s in New York City, and my latest novel The Spiral is a noir thriller set in that time and place with a heavy dose of memoir.

This novel is told through a fictional police report that slowly builds the fascinating account. The NYPD hired a wave of unconventional recruits meant to help the police department modernize. A young detective, Bo Lockley, assigned to the Times Square area, struggles with his idealism while working with the cynical veterans. He cannot stop the crime and destruction that occur around him, he is too innocent and the world is too dark.

But his occasional influence on the people around him, and the world’s impact on him, is the heart of the narrative. Both the book and the film carry the weight of the time. The film, directed by Milton Katselas and written by Abby Mann and Ernest Tidyman, has an outstanding cast, most notably Michael Moriarty and Yaphet Kotto, and the well-crafted script respects the original work.

Told from more than one perspective, Across 110th Street presents tragedies with realism, and emotional and sociopolitical depth. The robbery of an organized crime payroll puts the robbers, the police detectives, and the criminal drug lords in a triangle of pressure. In typical noir fashion, there is no way out, but the change that happens to the characters, as the story unfolds, gives the satisfying impact.

The compelling book reads like important historical testimony. Unfortunately, it is quite difficult to find a copy. The film, directed by Barry Shear and written by Luther Davis, is well made, magnificently portrayed by Yaphet Kotto and Anthony Quinn, extremely well-paced, and has an exceptional soundtrack.

Peter Maas, Frank Serpico, Serpico: The Classic Story of the Cop Who Couldn’t Be Bought

This nonfiction book is a critical account of the depth and complexity of corruption in the system of law and order from the time. It is an engaging biography of Frank Serpico whose background and personal history growing up in New York is an important precursor to the events that lead to the near tragic end.

While this story may only be considered on the fringe of noir, the historical background is essential reading to understand NYC noir fiction of the time. The film with Al Pacino as Serpico, directed by Sidney Lumet and written by Waldo Salt and Norman Wexler, is a superb visual representation, and should not be missed.

This novel was inspired by true events and starts at the very beginning of the life story of Theresa from the Bronx, a woman who has been on a downhill journey since childhood. Her life is articulated in a way that pulls us right alongside her, through her unlucky life events, misguided experiences, poor decision-making, and damaging self-treatment, all giving a realistic understanding of what it was like to live in that era. It is the full backstory of a dedicated teacher and lonely lost soul, in the film played brilliantly by Diane Keaton, as she consistently puts herself in dangerous situations that finally lead to the tragic ending.

Adapted for the screen and directed by Richard Brooks, he gives the story a thriller angle with a slightly different focus. Read the book first, and Theresa’s story will resonate even more forcefully.

Working class eighteen-year-old Stony is struggling to find himself in the macho construction worker world of his father and uncle, while trying to navigate the mental illness of his mother and little brother. In the dark confusion of his life, the social pressures, the family drama, he finds a glimmer of light when he discovers he has a talent and compassion for working with kids. But will the circumstances that surround him allow him to live the life he wants to live?

This 1970s noir portrait of a young man is beautifully drawn in the book, bringing us along with him on his rollercoaster journey. In the film, skillfully directed by Robert Mulligan and adapted for the screen by Walter Newman, Richard Gere gives an inspired performance as Stony and shares the screen with an excellent supporting cast.

Vincent Patrick, The Pope of Greenwich Village

Distant cousins Charlie and Paulie, living on the edge of organized crime, are two men who wouldn’t recognize a good decision if one fell on their heads. The interior lives of these two characters makes this book engaging as they struggle with their life choices forming a story that is more than a cautionary tale.

The film, directed by Stuart Rosenberg and adapted by the author, is more polished than many of its gritty counterparts, but it is worth watching, most especially for the performances of Mickey Roarke and Eric Roberts in their sparkling youth.

Lawrence Block, The Sins of the Fathers (Matthew Scudder Series #1)

The details and descriptions in Lawrence Block’s Matthew Scudder series are required reading when analyzing the 1970’s in New York City. Matthew Scudder is an ex-police detective, struggling with alcoholism and other demons. He’s no longer a cop, nor is he a licensed private investigator, but if someone asks nicely, and has cash to spend, he’ll take a case so he can pay the rent on his room at a flophouse and send money to his ex-wife and kids.

This first book is an interesting insight into a world of part-time sex workers and seedy lives on the fringe. The ending has a strange twist, but it is the haunting details of the lives of so many sad and lost individuals that make this story, and the entire series, essential reading for 70s noir exploration. Follow Matthew Scudder from the first to the last of the books in the series and watch him and New York City evolve.

Sadly, there is no adaptation for the screen of this novel. A few other books in the Matthew Scudder series were adapted for the screen but none of them retain the exquisite NYC 70s aspects so integral to the series.

Rosanne Limoncelli is an author, filmmaker, and storyteller living in Brooklyn. She has written, directed, and produced short narrative films, documentaries, and educational films. Rosanne also writes plays, screenplays, poetry, games, mysteries, and science fiction. Her short fiction has appeared in Alfred Hitchcock Mystery Magazine, Suspense Magazine and Noir Nation, and her short films have been screened in festivals around the world. The Four Queens of Crime is her debut mystery novel. Dr. Limoncelli has taught writing and filmmaking for more than three decades and is the Senior Director for Film Technologies at the Kanbar Institute and the Martin Scorsese Virtual Production Center at NYU’s Tisch School of the Arts.

#7674. Trial opens for suspect whose multiple email threats include ‘skinning’ federal judge

A series of threatening emails sent to the Northern District of California last year included “skinning U.S. District Judge Charles Breyer” and accused judges from the Golden State of being “enemy combatants.” (Image from Shutterstock)

A series of threatening emails sent to the Northern District of California last year included “skinning U.S. District Judge Charles Breyer” and accused judges from the Golden State of being “enemy combatants.”

David Brooks Pokorny, 45, of El Cerrito, California, allegedly sent 11 email threats in a span of 44 minutes to assault, kidnap and murder Breyer, a senior judge for the Northern District of California, according to U.S. Assistant Attorney Kent Stejskal in opening statements Tuesday.

“Words within those 11 emails constitute what are called true threats,” said Stejskal, according to coverage by Courthouse News Service.

He allowed the 14-person jury to view snippets of the emails during the trial. Pokorny is charged with making felony threats against a judicial officer and faces a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.

According to Pokorny’s public defender John Reichmuth, his client’s words were “truly shocking, truly offensive, truly ugly, but not true threats.”

Reichmuth said the emails were free speech, and the prosecution would have to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that Pokorny, who has a history of sending threats to public officials and media outlets, meant to perform the actions described in his emails.

Presiding U.S. District Judge Jon Tigar of the Northern District of California noted that the prosecution does not have to prove that Pokorny intended to carry out the threat for it to supersede the protections of First Amendment free speech rights.

#7673. 5 Infamous Women Killers and the Books You Should Read About Them

True Crime master and #1 New York Times bestselling author Gregg Olsen compiled his list of deadly women and the books written about them.

Read: Ordinary Wife: America’s Forgotten Serial Killer by Gregg Olsen and Morgan Olsen

Fittingly, the defense rested on Halloween 1921 in the case of arsenic poisoner Lyda Trueblood Dooley McHaffie Lewis Meyer Southard and the murders of her four dead husbands, a two-year-old daughter, and a brother-in-law. Lyda, like many other husband killers, murdered for insurance money. The tool of her trade? The arsenic she boiled off the flypaper.  Lyda made headlines as a femme fatale, a cold-blooded killer, and America’s Lady Bluebeard, and later, prison escapee.

Read: Hell’s Princess: The Mystery of Belle Gunness, Butcher of Men by Harold Schechter

If anything, Belle was direct. Very. She’d more likely smack a visitor over the head and feed them to the hogs on her Indiana Farm than use poison. She killed at least 14 people (including her husbands and children), though estimates go as high as 40 victims. Like Stella and Lyda, she did it for the money. She vanished when her farmhouse burned to the ground in 1908, spawning a mystery that has captivated true crime fans for more than a century. Did she get away with it?

Read: American Mother: The True Story of the Seattle Cyanide Killer by Gregg Olsen

Housewife and barfly, Stella Nickell had dreams bigger than her double-wide trailer. She concocted a scheme to kill her husband Bruce by reenacting the unsolved Chicago Tylenol cyanide poisonings. To make it appear a random act, she placed bottles of poison-laced headache capsules on grocery shelves, killing a mother of two, Sue Snow.

Former ambulance dispatcher Stacy Castor used antifreeze to kill two husbands. Michael was first, in 2000; his death was ruled a heart attack. Five years later, she staged husband David’s death as a suicide using a turkey baster as the implement to deliver the poison. Two years later, when suspicions turned into a bona fide investigation, Stacy tried to kill her daughter in order to keep her quiet. Not mom or wife of the year, for sure.

Nannie Doss takes the cake – at Halloween and in the annals of true crime. Indeed, the grandmother and frequent widow had a couple of those “ironic” nicknames – the “Giggling Granny” and the “Jolly Black Widow.” She seemed to enjoy the attention that her crimes brought. Nannie murdered at least 11 family members (four of whom were husbands) between 1927 and 1954 – making her America’s number one female murderer. No laughing matter by any stretch

Gregg Olsen is the #1 _New York Times_, #1 Amazon Charts, #1 _Wall Street Journal_, _Washington Post _and _USA Today_ bestselling author of more than 30 crime books. Based in rural Washington State, Olsen is a two-time Edgar Award-nominated author whose work has been honoured by the Mystery Writers of America and International Thriller Writers. His career has reached more than 8 million readers worldwide across print, ebook, audio, and Kindle Unlimited, including his breakout _hit If You Tell_, which spent more than 260 weeks in the Amazon Top 20.

#7672. DEI attacks are likely to refine and improve programs, experts say

The intense pressure to end diversity initiatives has led companies to scrutinize their policies. Many of the attacks will end up strengthening DEI programs.

The politicians, provocateurs and think tanks that in the past few years have worked to dismantle diversity, equity and inclusion may not appreciate the full consequences of their efforts.

They’ve used a variety of tactics, in the public and private sectors, including White House executive orders; lawsuits or the threat of lawsuits; shareholder proposals; and needling on social media. They’ve notched high-profile wins, most notably the Supreme Court’s ruling against affirmative action and capitulation at several companies, including retailers and brands that have ended or scaled back their DEI programs.

The successful challenges, inevitably, are forcing scrutiny of DEI practices. But they also provide an opportunity to reinforce DEI goals and execution, which David Glasgow, executive director of New York University’s Meltzer Center for Diversity, Inclusion, and Belonging, sees as a silver lining.

Indeed, the victories are hardly universal. Because diversity, equity and inclusion are good for business for a variety of reasons, most companies are not abandoning DEI. So far in 2025, Target, Nike and Costco are among those that have defended at least some aspects of their policies (in Costco’s case, vociferously). As the Heritage Foundation, a major DEI foe, noted in November, most Fortune 500 companies continue to publicly commit to DEI.

“It is a time for companies to refine and strengthen their inclusion efforts in ways that reduce the risk in the short term — because the risk is real, and we know that — and in ways that are sustainable in the long term,” said Adrienne Pulido, vice president of inclusion insights at Kantar. “So it is looking at both ends of the spectrum, in terms of being very clear about what inclusion means to their business.”

DEI is being pilloried as discriminatory and unfair, yet these systems are designed to create a business that is neither. That is, a business where employees have a variety of backgrounds and perspectives (diversity); hiring, promotion and other actions are executed fairly (equity); and the culture is comfortable and inviting to all who work there (inclusion).

“Unpacking what DEI is and what inclusion is, is part of this moment we're in and part of the conversation that companies need to have about their strategies,” Pulido said by video conference. “What does DEI mean to the business itself? What does it mean to the business and to the future business? Because the demographics of the country are changing, and our research shows that inclusion as a concept, as an idea, is very popular among Americans of all backgrounds.”

DEI goals for most companies are more important than ever because the markets for their products and services are more diverse than they were a decade or more ago, according to Effenus Henderson, who has worked in recruiting, staffing and succession planning at companies in the U.S. and abroad since the 1970s.

“This attack is amplified through the use of social media and technology and psychometrics, where emotions get aroused and reinforced,” he said by phone. “But fundamental to all this is that DEI is not about creating systems that are discriminatory, or about quotas, or a focus on one thing at the exclusion of others. I don't think organizations have really done that. What they have been doing is really trying to expand participation because of the growing demographic change that we're seeing.”

The need to develop DEI strategies that fit with and further business strategies dictates the involvement of leadership, according to Henderson. Too often, though, they are left to the human resources department, leaving companies at risk of adopting DEI programming that is ineffective and possibly indefensible.

“The companies that are able to navigate this generally are the ones where leadership has spent the time talking about it,” he said. “It's not just about reacting to the George Floyd situation or to civil rights laws or litigation. It's really, ‘How do we integrate this as a part of the DNA of who we are as an organization?’ If your organization is more performative, then they don't really understand how it helps to shape business strategy and policy.”

DEI should be treated like any other strategic priority, according to Tim Heneveld, country director for Pergolux in North America. With DEI under the spotlight, it’s a good moment to reassess whether hiring, workplace environment, leadership and operational strategies fit with broader aims.

“That means setting measurable goals, using data to track impact, and holding leadership accountable,” Heneveld said by email. “Some organizations are feeling pressure to scale back DEI, but I think doing so would be shortsighted. Instead, companies should refine their DEI strategies, aligning them with long-term business goals rather than reacting to what they are seeing in the media or any other outside factors. I've experienced, firsthand, workplaces can attract top talent, strengthen their teams, and improve retention.”

In some cases, companies are continuing with their DEI efforts, but changing the names of their initiatives or titles of their employees, experts said.

Crafting DEI initiatives and training is always a work in progress because businesses, markets and demographics evolve, according to Henderson. For many companies, that may mean avoiding those three letters of the alphabet, or the words “diversity, equity and inclusion.” But that, too, requires some thought, he said.

“Is continuing to refer to it under those banners still appropriate, and if I look at renaming it, am I doing that to help enhance our appeal to the markets of the customers and employees we serve? Are we doing it as a reactive, defensive thing for a short-term issue that's hot and heavy right now?” he said. “Get clarity around your objectives, the alignment with your strategies, and then decide whether how you are framing it today will work for you tomorrow and the day after. At some companies, it may mean one thing, and to others it may mean something else.”

The list of lawsuits against DEI programs tracked by the Meltzer Center is long, and getting longer.

Most of these claims invoke civil rights laws intended to end or prevent unfair hiring practices or contracts. Frequently that includes Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, barring discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex and national origin; Section 1981 of the federal code barring discrimination in contracts; and the U.S. Constitution’s equal protection clause, according to Glasgow. The Meltzer Center advises companies to avoid DEI practices that give preference to members of certain groups and involve a tangible benefit.

Evaluating whether a company’s DEI programs run afoul of the latest interpretations of these codes entails enlisting attorneys or other compliance experts.

“This has become a thriving legal practice area,” Glasgow said.

Any business strategy should always be grounded in risk mitigation, and this is just another place for companies to check, according to Henderson. Companies may learn that, to avoid risk, certain aspects of their DEI programs should change.

Others may find that they pass muster. In its proxy statement urging shareholders to vote against a proposal that could have weakened its DEI programs, Costco’s board of directors made clear that the retailer regularly evaluates its “practices concerning compliance with law, including evolving Supreme Court decisions.”

In describing how Costco obeys the law and does not discriminate in hiring, promotion and other practices, the board also provided a litany of protected statuses. This is a reminder that, while civil rights statutes are being leveraged to overturn DEI practices, they nevertheless do bar discrimination for a host of reasons. Moreover, any company that does business abroad will encounter antidiscrimination law that isn’t being disrupted by political activism the way it is in the U.S., Henderson said.

“If you look at Canada, Europe, Asia and South America, there are regulations and laws that support and value diversity,” he said. “So backing away from DEI may, in fact, create harm for your business strategies in other parts of the world. It's not a simple answer, and it just depends on who you are.”

While it may seem like DEI programs are quickly getting scrapped in order to avoid controversy, most are simply under review, Glasgow and others said.

“I think it's prompting a much deeper reflection within companies, not just on what is strictly legal or illegal in what we're doing, but on what has been working and what has not been working,” Glasgow said. “Could we be doing this work more effectively, in a way that actually helps us achieve our business goals, or helps us create the kind of culture that we want to create? Are there things that have been low impact, or maybe even have a negative impact, that we should get rid of, even if it's not for legal reasons? I think the moment that we're living in now could be a helpful reset moment for the field.”
