#7582. Court to hear argument on whether and when federal officials can be held liable for violations of the Constitution

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court will hear oral argument on Monday, Nov. 9, in a lawsuit brought by a Hawaii man, Kekai Watanabe, who contends that a prison paramedic violated his constitutional rights when he failed to provide medical treatment after Watanabe was injured during a fight while in federal custody. Both the paramedic, Francis Nielsen, and the Trump administration, which filed a “friend of the court” brief supporting Nielsen, urge the justices to shut down Watanabe’s case; Nielsen also suggests that the court should go even further and foreclose efforts to recover from federal officials for violations of the Constitution.

More than 50 years ago, in Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of Federal Bureau of Narcotics, the Supreme Court ruled that a violation of an individual’s constitutional rights by a federal official can create a federal claim for damages.

In the years that followed, the justices have extended their decision in Bivens only twice. In Davis v. Passman, in 1979, the court held that a former congressional staffer could sue a member of Congress for alleged sex discrimination in violation of the Fifth Amendment. And in Carlson v. Green, the court held that the estate of an inmate, who died after having an asthma attack, could bring a Bivens claim when prison officials had failed to provide adequate medical care for eight hours after the attack and did not send him to the hospital during that time.

But since then the court has resisted efforts to rely on Bivens. Four years ago, in Egbert v. Boule, it observed that it had “declined 11 times to imply a similar cause of action for other alleged constitutional violations” and that “in all but the most unusual circumstances, prescribing a cause of action is a job for Congress, not the courts.” Moreover, Justice Clarence Thomas noted for the majority “that if we were called to decide Bivens today, we would decline to discover any implied causes of action in the Constitution. But,” Thomas wrote, “to decide the case before us, we need not reconsider Bivens itself.”

In the present case, Watanabe was badly injured during a gang-related fight while at a federal detention center in Hawaii. He contends that he told Nielsen, who treated him, that his pain was a 10 on a scale of 1 to 10, but Nielsen gave him only over-the-counter pain medication. Watanabe alleges that he was kept in solitary confinement for more than two months, during which he did not see a specialist or go to a hospital. When Watanabe eventually obtained an x-ray seven months later, it revealed that he had a fractured coccyx and that chips from the bone had penetrated the soft tissue in the area. He says that he continues to be in “tremendous pain.”

In February 2022, Watanabe went to federal court in Honolulu. Relying on Bivens and Carlson, he alleged that Nielsen violated his rights under the Eighth Amendment to be free of cruel and unusual punishment because Nielsen was deliberately indifferent to his serious medical needs.

The district court dismissed Watanabe’s claim. It held that Carlson did not apply because his claim arose in a new context – that is, it was not sufficiently similar to the facts of that case for his claim to go forward.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit reversed. It acknowledged that the Supreme Court “has cautioned against extending Bivens remedies to new contexts,” but in its view “Watanabe’s claim is identical to Carlson in all meaningful respects” and therefore can proceed. A deeply divided court of appeals declined to rehear the case.

Nielsen appealed to the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear the case in June.

In his brief on the merits, Nielsen contends that Watanabe’s case fails both prongs of the “demanding two-part test” that the Supreme Court has established for Bivens claims. That test, he adds, boils down to “whether there is any reason to think Congress might be better equipped to create a damages remedy.”

The first question is whether the claim arises in a new context from the three cases in which it has recognized Bivens claims. “Even ‘small’ differences from the original Bivens trio” of cases “will present a new context,” Nielsen writes: “‘a modest extension is still an extension.’” Watanabe’s claim, Nielsen argues, is not modest but is instead “meaningfully—profoundly—different” from Carlson. As an initial matter, he says, the facts are markedly dissimilar, because the inmate in Carlson died just hours after the attack, so that monetary compensation for his estate was the only possible remedy. By contrast, Nielsen asserts, Watanabe’s “injury was neither fatal nor life-threatening,” and instead of monetary damages he could have sought more treatment or a move to a hospital through either internal prison appeals or by filing a lawsuit in court.

If the context is new, Nielsen continues, the next question is whether “there are ‘special factors’ indicating that” courts are “at least arguably less equipped than Congress to ‘weigh the costs and benefits of allowing a damages action to proceed.’ ‘If there is even a single “reason to pause before applying Bivens in a new context,” a court may not recognize a Bivens remedy.’” Nielsen points to at least two “special factors” at play in this case that “‘suggest[] that Congress did [not] want’” prisoners to be able to recover monetary compensation from federal officials. First, he said, the Administrative Remedy Program – a grievance process created by the Bureau of Prisons in 1979 – “provides an alternative remedial structure for federal prisoners.” Second, he added, the Prison Litigation Reform Act, enacted in 1996, requires prisoners to use all available internal prison appeals like the ARP before going to court.

Nielsen further tells the justices that they should throw out not only Watanabe’s claim but Bivens along with it. Bivens, Davis, and Carlson, he says, “are relics of the bygone days when federal courts thought it appropriate to create causes of action congress had not authorized.”

The federal government sides with Nielsen to the extent that he argues that Watanabe’s claim should be thrown out. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer tells the court that “Carlson has become entirely obsolete” in light of new laws like the PLRA and the creation of the ARP. “And given courts’ lack of authority and expertise in setting prison policy,” Sauer said, “courts will always have a reason to pause before extending Carlson to that new context. That means that no more Carlson claims will be viable.” But, Sauer continues, the court should decline Nielsen’s suggestion to “consider overruling Bivens in this case. If the Court wishes to consider that question,” Sauer writes, “it should do so in the context of a Fourth Amendment case that more closely resembles Bivens itself.”

In his brief, Watanabe insists that his case “arises in th[e] prototypical Carlson context.” “It is,” he writes, “a damages action against a federal prison officer who was deliberately indifferent to a federal prisoner’s serious medical needs in violation of the Eighth Amendment.” Moreover, he continues, both his claim and the claim in Carlson involved “the same kind of defendant in the same kind of federal institution under the same legal framework.” The fact that he suffered from a different medical problem than Carlson, or that the inmate in Carlson died while Watanabe survived does not make his case a “new context,” he argues. Instead, he contends, such differences “are case-specific, factual variations to which” Carlson’s “settled rule applies.”

Watanabe pushes back against Nielsen’s contention that, because he is still alive, he (unlike the inmate in Carlson) also has other remedies available to him. Only money, he says, can compensate him for “his past pain and suffering.”

Watanabe tells the justices that, contrary to Nielsen’s suggestion, Congress has indicated that claims like his and the one in Carlson should be allowed to go forward, albeit with some restrictions. He points first to the Westfall Act, a 1988 law that stripped prisoners of their ability to sue federal officers under state law for their injuries, but specifically carved out an exception for “federal constitutional claims like those in Carlson.” And although the Prison Litigation Reform Act requires prisoners to pursue all of their internal appeals “before pursuing a Carlson claim,” it nonetheless shows, Watanabe argues, that Congress intended for Carlson claims to be available.

Watanabe urges the justices to leave Carlson in place even if the court might reach a different decision today. Among other things, he argues, that decision “was not egregiously wrong” and Congress has relied on it in fashioning remedies for inmates – two factors that courts consider when deciding whether to overturn their prior cases. And more broadly, he contends, if the Supreme Court were to overrule Carlson, it “would create a novel situation, never contemplated by Congress, in which federal prisoners who are subjected to needless suffering in violation of the Eighth Amendment have no recourse against the responsible officers.”

A decision in the case is expected sometime next year.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

In the aftermath of Election Day, Republicans and Democrats alike are grappling with what the blue wave means for the Supreme Court. Keep reading to learn how the Senate shake-up, in particular, could affect when a justice next leaves the court and how the confirmation process might unfold.

Plus, one year ago today, the justices heard argument in Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, a challenge to President Donald Trump’s tariff regime. Just over three months later, the Supreme Court struck down the tariffs, holding that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act does not give the president the authority to impose tariffs.

On Wednesday, the justices heard argument in Guerrero v. Johnson, on the limited circumstances in which a state prisoner can return to federal court for a second round of post-conviction review.

Tomorrow, the justices will meet in a private conference to discuss cases and vote on petitions for review. Orders from Friday’s conference are expected on Monday at 9:30 a.m. EST.

On Oct. 21, the Trump administration asked the justices to allow it to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. The request is now fully briefed, and the court’s decision could come at any time.

#7579. Court to consider the reach of Article III courts in immigration contract dispute

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The argument on Nov. 10 in Department of Labor v. Sun Valley Orchards brings the justices a complex constitutional problem sure to get their focused attention: does the Constitution allow Congress to delegate to the executive branch – as opposed to the courts – the authority to adjudicate the obligation of an employer to comply with employment agreements it makes with temporary immigrant workers.

Here, the Department of Labor, employing administrative law judges, for several decades has adjudicated disputes under the H-2A visa program, which allows employers to hire temporary foreign agricultural workers. The Department of Labor argues that Sun Valley Orchards failed in several ways to compensate such workers as it promised the government it would to qualify for the H-2A program. As is typical in such cases, administrative employees of the DOL (in its wage and hour division) charged Sun Valley with failing to live up to its obligations, and the DOL for the most part persuaded an ALJ that it was correct. On appeal, a different group of the DOL’s employees (its administrative review board) accepted the ALJ’s findings. At that point, for the first time, Sun Valley had a chance to take the dispute before Article III judges, but under the applicable statute the federal district court owes great deference to the DOL’s adjudication.

The case comes to the justices because the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit reasoned that the administrative adjudication of the department’s charges cannot be reconciled with Article III of the Constitution.

At a high level of generality, the doctrinal framework here is quite clear. All agree that Congress constitutionally can authorize adjudication by executive branch officials rather than judges, and all agree that its power to do so is limited to cases that involve “public rights,” a notoriously vague category designed to distinguish traditionally executive actions (like granting a visa) from disputes traditionally resolved in court (like tort and contract litigation). When those adjudications go beyond public rights, though, they infringe on the judiciary’s exclusive authority under Article III. The difficulty is that when you get down to details – defining the boundaries of “public rights” – the rulings have neither been stable nor persuasive. The point was made best by Chief Justice William Rehnquist (channeling Matthew Arnold), who famously characterized the decisions as “landmarks on a judicial ‘darkling plain’ where ignorant armies have clashed by night.”

For this particular dispute, the government contends that the case plainly involves public rights because it involves immigration or because it involves the assessment of remedies for transgression of privileges granted by the executive. By contrast, the employer characterizes the subject of the adjudication as a contract dispute. Granting the government’s free ability to decide (and adjudicate if it wishes to do so) the entitlement of any particular immigrants or group of immigrants to a visa or other immigration status, the dispute here involves whether the employer has complied with its employment contract. Because that is a prototypically private dispute – the kind of thing that could have been brought before a court at Westminster in Old England in the days of the drafting of Article III – the employer contends that it is not the kind of public right that Congress can have adjudicated by the executive.

It would be naïve to expect the justices will feel themselves constrained by the existing precedents on this topic. The case directly implicates the prerogatives of the judicial branch and the justices will see it that way. Moreover, decisions like Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo and Trump v. Slaughter show a bench with a great appetite for reining in the administrative state even when precedents are settled and directly on point. And there is another problem for the government here – many of the cases they rely on predate the days of FDR and the rise of the administrative state. Furthermore, none of them crisply validates an administrative adjudication that takes money from one private party and gives it to another.

I would expect Justice Neil Gorsuch to be a major figure at the argument, as he has been pressing this particular point for several years, albeit in the context of the securities laws. For him, the government’s contention that the lower court decision would disrupt a large swath of long-accepted administrative arrangements will be a feature, not a bug. Chief Justice John Roberts also can be expected to be an important player, as he has written several of the modern opinions in the area. So this seemingly narrow dispute may herald something larger: yet another blow against the administrative state.

Ronald Mann is a professor of law at Columbia, where he teaches courses in commercial finance, payment systems and deals.

#7578. Gun-owners fight assault rifle ban at Supreme Court of Canada

Canada banned firearms like the AR-15 and the Ruger Mini-14 rifle in the wake of a shooting in Nova Scotia in 2020 that killed nearly two dozen people.

OTTAWA, Ontario (CN) â Firearm enthusiasts in Canada are trying to reverse a ban introduced by the federal government in May 2020 prohibiting the ownership and importation of 1,500 models of firearms and their variants, claiming that Ottawa exceeded its legal authority.

Four different appeals of the ban have been combined for the hearings in front of Canada’s highest court on Monday and Tuesday.

Christine Generoux, a woman from Ottawa representing herself, is leading the appellate campaign. She is supported by hunters, Indigenous people and sports and firearm advocates.

The gun rights activists are arguing that the broad policy, notably banning the use of AR-15 and Ruger Mini-14Â rifles, has made weapons illegal that have always been used safely by hunters and sports amateurs, and even Olympic athletes.

Generoux said that the ban prohibits firearms that could cause harm to another person, but that could apply to any weapon, and could lead to more restrictions for gun owners in the future.

She claimed that firearms enthusiasts were being unduly targeted and painted as criminals for their hobby by the government, saying that they were “using our community as scapegoats to cover for their own poor public policy.”

The ban was introduced in the wake of a deadly mass shooting that caused 23 deaths â including the shooter â in Nova Scotia in April 2020. A month later, then-Prime Minister Justin Trudeau announced that military-grade assault weapons would be prohibited.

The prime minister’s Cabinet policy is considered an Order in Council â equivalent to a U.S. president’s executive order â and has therefore not been ratified by Parliament. The Criminal Code grants power to the Cabinet to enact restrictions regarding firearms if itÂ deems that the weapons cannot reasonably be used for hunting and sports shooting.

Counsel for the Canadian Coalition for Firearm Rights, Michael A. Loberg, argued that the ban targeted weapons that historically have been used for hunting and sports, and that the Cabinet had overreached its legal authority and violated the mandate Parliament had granted it to restrict firearms.

The case was previously dismissed by the Federal Court and the Federal Court of Appeal, which had both deemed that the government has used valid arguments regarding public safety to justify the ban.

The nine justices of the top court also questioned if the weapon owners had sufficiently considered the weight of public safety in the balance that the government tried to strike with firearms enthusiasts’ interests.

“I can see that many of these weapons, despite their potential danger, can be used safely,” Justice Glenn D.Â Joyal said. “In some instances, at some point in time, suddenly, irrespective of how safely the weapon is being used by a sports person, others are using it in a very different way.”

The attorney general of Canada defended the policy, arguing that only 3% to 5%Â of gun owners would be affected by the ban, and that plenty of other firearms were available for hunting and sport shooting.

“Is it reasonable to allow these guns to continue to be used in Canada for hunting and sporting purposes, given the risk of enormous harms they can cause if they get into the wrong hands?” attorney Zoe Oxaal said.

The justices sought many clarifications from attorney general regarding the policy and its wide reach, but they seemed to agree that the government had acted lawfully.

“There may be cases where perhaps the [Government in Council] has gone too far, but that’s different than saying the whole shebang is defective,” said Justice Mahmud Jamal, claiming that the ban on some models could be contested individually, if necessary.

The current ban is suspended until the Supreme Court ruling comes out. If the justices uphold the policy, Canadians who own the firearm models and variants included in the ban will have an amnesty period of 90 days to dispose of or permanently deactivate their weapons.

A buyback program established to help businesses and individuals be compliant with the law has collected almost 75,000 weapons as of mid-2026, and businesses have received 96 million Canadian dollars ($67 million) in compensation for their participation.

The hearing will continue Tuesday, with firearms and sports associations expected to intervene in favor of the plaintiffs, as well as three conservative provincial governments opposing the ban: Alberta, Ontario and Saskatchewan.

Courthouse News reporter Tatiana Mulowayi-Pelletier is based in Montreal, Canada.

#7577. Lindsay Clancy loses bid to dismiss murder case, teeing up retrial

After her first case ended in a mistrial, Clancy argued it would be double jeopardy to try her again for killing her three young children.

(CN) â A Massachusetts judge on Monday denied Lindsay Clancyâs motion to dismiss her triple-murder case, paving the way for the 36-year-old to be tried again.

In a 17-page ruling, Plymouth Superior Court Judge William Sullivan found a retrial in this case wouldnât be considered double jeopardy since her initial jury deadlocked.

âA hung jury is a traditional example of manifest necessity that permits retrial without offending double jeopardy,â Sullivan wrote.

Clancy, who stood trial this year for strangling her three young children to death in 2023, had her first case end in a mistrial after one holdout juror prevented an acquittal. Clancy says she was experiencing postpartum psychosis and that she should be found not guilty by reason of insanity.

After a contentious deliberation process, 11 of the 12 jurors were prepared to accept that argument. They wrote in notes to the court that the holdout, who has since been identified as Michael Desronvil, didnât follow the courtâs instructions on reasonable doubt and was steadfast in his vote to convict Clancy.

Clancy argued at a hearing last week that the judge should have probed the jury to see if there was good cause to dismiss Desronvil â referred to as âJuror Doeâ throughout the proceedings.

Sullivan ruled on that, too, in his Monday order. He found the record âdid not reasonably suggest Juror Doeâs inability to deliberate or refusal to follow the law.â

âClancy cites numerous cases in which it was deemed appropriate to question a juror based on a note suggesting an inability to deliberate,â Sullivan wrote. âHowever, those cases involved notes which were quite specific â¦ and in many cases, the notes quoted detailed comments from the juror himself expressing an inability or unwillingness to deliberate.â

It wasnât all bad news for the defense, though. Sullivan issued a separate ruling rejecting state prosecutorsâ request for a gag order, after they argued Clancyâs defense attorneys disparaged Desronvil in news conferences and made other prejudicial statements about the case.

Sullivan found the state failed to meet the high bar that would justify such a so-called âprior restraintâ order on the attorneysâ speech.

âA prior restraint can only be justified by a compelling state interest to protect against a serious threat of harm,â the judge wrote. âThe commonwealth has not sufficiently demonstrated that defense counselâs extrajudicial speech poses a serious threat of harm by materially prejudicing the jury venire or the outcome of any retrial.â

However, Sullivan added the state can seek this remedy again if the circumstances change.

The Plymouth County District Attorneyâs Office declined to comment on Mondayâs rulings. Clancyâs legal team didnât immediately respond to a request for comment.

Sullivanâs rulings came a week after the parties reconvened in his courtroom for a motions hearing on these issues. It was there that prosecutors told the judge they would seek to try Clancy again for killing her three children, though it remains unclear specifically what charges she would face.

âThis would be a retrial,â Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague told the court on Nov. 2. âAs to what that looks like, it will depend. Weâre not at that point yet.â

Clancy initially faced three counts of murder after she admitted to fatally strangling her 5-year-old daughter Cora, 3-year-old son Dawson and 8-month-old son Callan while in the midst of postpartum psychosis. She then cut her wrists and neck and jumped from a second-floor window in an apparent suicide attempt that paralyzed her from the waist down.

Her legal team said last week she is on constant suicide watch and still has nightmares about the incident. She remains in custody at Tewksbury Hospital, a Massachusetts psychiatric facility about 20 miles north of Boston.

The parties are reconvening early next week to discuss the caseâs next steps. Sullivan floated a retrial date of March 2027.

#7575. Who Is Elena Kagan? Ideology, strategy, and the art of disagreement

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

On May 21, 2026, Justice Elena Kagan did something she had never done in nearly 16 years on the Supreme Court: she dissented alone in a signed decision. The case, Havana Docks v. Royal Caribbean Cruises, concerned whether cruise lines could face liability for using Cuban docks confiscated decades earlier. Eight justices, including Kagan’s liberal colleagues Sonia Sotomayor and Ketanji Brown Jackson, sided against the cruise lines. Kagan thought the majority had misunderstood a basic principle of property law: the interest originally confiscated had expired long before the cruise ships arrived.

The solitary dissent was unusual for a justice who has spent much of her tenure avoiding separate opinions. At a judicial conference in July 2025, Kagan observed that the court “speaks best when it speaks as a court,” and acknowledged that she sometimes drafts dissents only to decide against publishing them.

Kagan’s professional background is also unusual. She is the only current justice who arrived at the Supreme Court without previously serving as a judge. Before her appointment in 2010, she had been a law professor, dean of Harvard Law School, a White House adviser, and solicitor general of the United States. Her career was therefore shaped substantially by institutions in which persuasion, negotiation, and managing competing perspectives are routine.

But how much does this explain her jurisprudence? Ideological measures generally place Kagan to the right of her liberal colleagues, and her voting record contains meaningful differences from Sotomayor’s and Jackson’s. Yet those differences are far from uniform, and Kagan’s reluctance to write separately persists even when she reaches precisely the same result as her colleagues.

Understanding Kagan therefore requires examining not only how she votes, but how she chooses to agree and disagree.

Kagan has generally occupied a position to the right of the other liberal justices in measures of Supreme Court ideology. But the distance between them depends considerably on how ideology is measured, which cases are examined, and when the comparison is made.

The best-known measure is the Martin–Quinn score, which estimates the justices’ ideological positions from their voting patterns over time. In the 2024-25 term, Kagan’s score was −1.85, compared with −2.80 for Jackson and −4.19 for Sotomayor. Kagan was thus the rightmost of the three liberals, although she remained substantially to the left of the court’s median justice, Amy Coney Barrett, whose score was +0.53. The estimates for Jackson and Kagan had been closer in earlier terms (and, in fact, Jackson was initially positioned slightly to Kagan’s right).

The scores capture something revealing about how the justices vote, but they do not directly measure the substance of their legal reasoning or their willingness to compromise. Nor does a justice’s location relative to the other liberals necessarily reveal whether her own jurisprudence has changed. Martin–Quinn estimates are relative positions derived from voting coalitions, and those coalitions are themselves influenced by the court’s membership and docket.

The voting record offers a more concrete comparison. During the 2010–2021 terms, there were 56 contested decisions in which Kagan joined the majority while Sotomayor dissented, compared with just 19 in which their positions were reversed. Kagan was nearly three times as likely to be on the prevailing side when the two disagreed. That is a substantial difference, although it does not establish that every disagreement reflected an ideological division.

Justice Stephen Breyer, long considered a moderate liberal on the court, provides a useful point of reference. During their overlapping time on the court, Kagan joined the majority without Breyer 41 times, while Breyer joined the majority without Kagan 31 times. The more balanced relationship suggests that Kagan’s historical voting behavior often resembled Breyer’s more closely than Sotomayor’s.

The picture has changed since Jackson joined the court in 2022. Across 121 contested decisions in which Kagan and Sotomayor both participated through the 2025 term, they voted on the same side 109 times. Kagan prevailed without Sotomayor seven times, while Sotomayor prevailed without Kagan five times. Their historical difference in majority participation has thus narrowed dramatically.

The convergence is particularly visible in closely divided cases. Of 82 decisions decided 5–4 or 6–3 in which Kagan, Sotomayor, and Jackson all participated, the three liberals voted together in 71. When the court divided most sharply, Kagan usually found herself alongside her liberal colleagues rather than occupying a position between the liberal and conservative wings.

There are then two different stories in the numbers. Over much of her tenure, Kagan was more likely than Sotomayor to support outcomes favored by conservative justices. More recently, that distinction has diminished, particularly in closely divided cases. Whether this reflects a change in Kagan’s jurisprudence or the changing opportunities for cross-ideological agreement remains uncertain.

The cases in which she breaks with her liberal colleagues offer a way to examine that distinction more closely.

One way to identify a comparatively moderate justice is to examine how frequently she votes with colleagues across the ideological divide. By that measure, Kagan has demonstrated considerable independence from her liberal colleagues.

Across 26 terms, Kagan was the only liberal voting alongside conservative justices in 27 contested decisions, approximately 5.3% of her non-unanimous votes. Sotomayor occupied that position in 18 decisions, or 3.4%. Yet Breyer did so in 29 cases, representing 7.1% of his contested votes during the years he served alongside Kagan. When he was on the court, Breyer, rather than Kagan, was more likely to separate from the other liberals in that way.

The pattern becomes even more interesting with Jackson’s arrival. During the 2022–2025 terms, Kagan was the sole liberal voting with conservatives in nine contested cases, compared with ten for Jackson (though this frequency has decreased) and just two for Sotomayor. Jackson’s cross-ideological votes were evenly divided between joining majorities and dissents, while Kagan’s predominantly placed her in the majority. Thus, even when two justices cross ideological lines with similar frequency, they may not be doing the same thing.

These voting coalitions also raise a question about Kagan’s reputation as a consensus-builder. Does she actually attract more conservative support when writing for the court?

The analysis provides surprisingly little evidence that she does. Of Kagan’s 47 majority opinions in contested decisions, 27 attracted at least three conservative votes. Sotomayor achieved the same result in 30 of her 49 contested majority opinions. Their records are then similar, suggesting that Kagan’s reputation for building agreement is not necessarily reflected in a distinctive ability to assemble ideologically diverse majorities.

The individual cases also complicate the idea that Kagan’s departures from the liberal wing are simply strategic compromises. In 2020’s Kahler v. Kansas, for example, Kagan wrote for six justices, including five conservatives, holding that the Constitution does not require states to recognize an insanity defense based on a defendant’s inability to distinguish right from wrong. Breyer, joined by Ginsburg and Sotomayor, dissented. Kagan emphasized the historical diversity of insanity rules and the latitude afforded to state legislatures; Breyer saw Kansas’s approach as eliminating a fundamental protection deeply rooted in criminal law.

Four years later, Pulsifer v. United States presented a dispute over the meaning of a single conjunction in a federal sentencing statute. Kagan wrote for a six-justice majority, including five conservatives, adopting a reading that restricted defendants’ eligibility for relief from mandatory minimum sentences. Gorsuch dissented, joined by Sotomayor and Jackson, favoring an interpretation that would have made relief more widely available.

Neither case is easily explained as Kagan merely accommodating conservative colleagues and both show substantive disagreements over the meaning of legal rules, with significant consequences for criminal defendants.

These decisions also show why ideological distance and judicial method cannot be treated as interchangeable. Kagan’s cross-ideological votes sometimes reflect legal commitments that produce outcomes different from those favored by her liberal colleagues. They also suggest that her willingness to build agreement does not automatically lead her toward the narrowest available resolution.

If Kagan is not consistently more successful than Sotomayor at attracting conservative votes, the more distinctive feature of her jurisprudence may lie elsewhere: what she does after reaching agreement, and particularly when she decides that a disagreement warrants an opinion of her own.

The art of agreement: choosing when to write

The most distinctive feature of Kagan’s judicial behavior may have less to do with how she votes than with how she expresses agreement. During her 16 terms on the court, Kagan authored just 18 concurrences in signed decisions, compared with 81 for Sotomayor. Breyer, often described as an institutionally minded pragmatist, also wrote concurrences at more than twice Kagan’s rate during their overlapping service. Jackson has been considerably more prolific in her shorter tenure. Kagan’s comparative restraint is therefore striking even among justices who share many of her substantive positions.

The difference becomes even more revealing when the comparison is limited to cases in which the justices reached exactly the same outcome. Between 2010 and 2021, Kagan and Sotomayor both supported a conservative-authored majority opinion in 93 contested decisions. Sotomayor wrote separately in 13 of those cases; Kagan did so in just one. The difference is difficult to explain through ideology or case selection alone: the two justices were participating in the same decisions, agreeing with the same majorities, yet approaching the question of whether to write separately very differently.

The distinction has narrowed somewhat in recent years, but it has not vanished. During the 2022–2025 terms, Kagan wrote separately in three of 38 conservative-authored majorities she shared with Sotomayor, compared with five for Sotomayor. In 29 comparable cases involving Kagan and Jackson, Kagan wrote separately twice and Jackson eight times. These samples are smaller, but they reinforce the larger finding that Kagan is particularly reluctant to add her individual voice to an outcome she already supports.

Kagan herself has offered a remarkably candid explanation for this. Speaking at the 9th Circuit Judicial Conference in July 2025, she described the Supreme Court as an institution whose opinions should communicate a collective judgment. She acknowledged that producing a single institutional voice requires “a little bit of flexibility and compromise.” Separate opinions, she suggested, can complicate the law by presenting competing explanations of what the court has supposedly decided.

Yet Kagan’s restraint should not be mistaken for unqualified agreement. In 2024’s United States v. Rahimi, she joined Roberts’ majority upholding a federal restriction on firearm possession by individuals subject to certain domestic violence restraining orders. She also joined Sotomayor’s concurrence, which defended the majority’s application of New York State Rifle & Pistol Association Inc. v. Bruen while reiterating their disagreement with that earlier Second Amendment decision holding there to be a constitutional right to carry a firearm. Jackson wrote her own concurrence addressing the difficulties lower courts had encountered applying Bruen. All three liberals agreed with the outcome, but their choices about authorship differed.

A similar pattern appeared in 2023’s National Pork Producers Council v. Ross, in which the court rejected an argument by pork producers that a law violated the Constitution by regulating the pork industry outside of California. Kagan joined Sotomayor’s separate opinion explaining why they agreed with the judgment without embracing portions of Gorsuch’s reasoning that threatened to alter the established constitutional framework. Kagan was willing to register a qualification, but she did so by joining a colleague’s opinion rather than writing another.

These distinctions again complicate the portrayal of Kagan as a consensus-builder. The data do not show that she consistently attracts more conservative support to her own majority opinions than Sotomayor does. They show something different: Kagan is considerably more selective about articulating separate disagreements when she already supports the court’s disposition. That behavior may preserve a clearer institutional message, but it also leaves fewer public indication of her reservations about particular decisions.

The difference matters when interpreting Kagan’s ideological position. A justice who joins an opinion without writing separately may appear closer to its author than one who publishes a concurrence, even when both share the same substantive objection. Kagan’s record suggests the absence of a separate opinion can reflect a decision about judicial expression rather than any lack of disagreement.

The limits of agreement: textualism, precedent, and dissent

Kagan’s willingness to work across ideological lines has never meant avoiding deep disagreements with the court’s conservatives. Some of her sharpest opinions have challenged not only their conclusions but also their fidelity to the interpretive principles they profess to follow.

In a 2015 lecture at Harvard Law School honoring Antonin Scalia, Kagan famously remarked, “We’re all textualists now.” The observation acknowledged Scalia’s influence on statutory interpretation, including among justices who did not share his ideological commitments. Seven years later, in her dissent in West Virginia v. EPA, Kagan explicitly revisited that statement: “It seems I was wrong.”

Her objection concerned the majority’s use of the major questions doctrine to restrict the Environmental Protection Agency’s authority under the Clean Air Act. Kagan argued that the court had departed from ordinary statutory interpretation by demanding an unusually clear congressional authorization for agency action of substantial economic or political significance. In her account, the conservative majority’s claimed commitment to textualism yielded when the statutory text pointed toward an outcome it disfavored.

The exchange is revealing because Kagan was challenging the majority from within a methodology often associated with conservative jurisprudence. Her embrace of textualism did not entail agreement with the conservatives about what particular statutes meant, much less about how much authority courts should exercise over Congress and administrative agencies.

That distinction became even clearer in 2024’s Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo. Writing for the three liberals, subject to Jackson’s recusal in one of the consolidated cases, Kagan defended Chevron deference (deferring to agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes) against the majority’s decision to overrule it. Her argument rested on statutory interpretation, congressional allocation of authority, administrative expertise, and the importance of precedent (a common theme for her). Textualism, in Kagan’s jurisprudence, does not necessarily require courts to resolve every statutory ambiguity without deference to an agency authorized to administer the law.

The same institutional concerns appear in her criticism of the court’s emergency docket. In Trump v. Wilcox, Kagan dissented from an order permitting the administration, pending further litigation, to remove officials from independent agencies. Joined by Sotomayor and Jackson, she objected both to the treatment of longstanding precedent and to the use of an expedited proceeding to alter the practical operation of existing law without ordinary briefing and argument.

These opinions provide an important counterweight to Kagan’s reputation for accommodation. Her restraint in writing separately does not preclude forceful disagreement when she believes the court has departed from established interpretive or institutional principles. Nor does that pattern necessarily distinguish her substantive positions from those of Sotomayor and Jackson, who joined these dissents.

The recurring question is therefore not simply whether Kagan is willing to compromise but where she draws the line between disagreements she can accommodate and those that she considers important enough to articulate publicly.

Sixteen years of decisions reveal a justice whose reputation for moderation captures only part of her judicial behavior. Kagan has historically been more willing than Sotomayor to join conservative-supported outcomes, and some of those differences reflect genuine disagreements about the law. Yet the gap has narrowed considerably in recent terms, particularly in cases that divide the court along ideological lines.

What distinguishes Kagan more consistently is her approach to disagreement. She is not uniquely successful at attracting conservative votes to her majority opinions. Rather, she is unusually reluctant to write separately when she can support an existing opinion, even in cases where her liberal colleagues reach the same result but feel compelled to explain their reservations. Her willingness to join another justice’s concurrence further complicates any assumption that silence necessarily signifies agreement.

The distinction has become more consequential as the court has moved rightward. Kagan’s opportunities to assemble majorities across ideological lines have diminished, while her dissents in disputes over administrative authority, precedent, and institutional power have become an increasingly public part of her jurisprudence.

Whether those patterns reflect a conscious strategy, enduring professional instincts, or some combination of the two cannot be determined from voting records alone. But the comparisons suggest that understanding Kagan requires looking beyond where she falls on an ideological scale. Her place on the court is defined both by the legal positions she takes and by the choices she makes about when – and how – to express them.

Dr. Adam Feldman is the creator and author of the blog Empirical SCOTUS and the Substack Legalytics.

#7571. St. Mary and the shrinking reach of Smith

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Justice Clarence Thomas began Colorado’s half of the argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy with a pointed observation. In the court’s last two cases about religious schools and public benefits, Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue and Carson v. Makin, the justices “did not use, even cite, Smith.” So, he asked Colorado’s deputy solicitor general, “Why would we do that in this case?”

That question goes to the heart of the case. After argument, it would be surprising if Colorado won. The real fight is over how the Catholic preschools win. And the answer will determine how much is left of Employment Division v. Smith, perhaps the court’s most contested free exercise precedent.

In 2020, Colorado voters approved funding for universal preschool. The program that followed pays for 15 hours a week of preschool for every four-year-old in the state, worth about $6,300 per child. Families can spend that money at roughly 2,000 participating preschools: public, private, and religious. Every provider must accept an “equal opportunity” mandate. Specifically, children must have an equal opportunity to enroll “regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability.”

The mandate is not absolute. Colorado lets preschools use enrollment “preferences” for, among other things, children of employees, siblings, members of a specific community, and families willing to volunteer. More than 1,000 preschools use at least one. But Catholic parish preschools in the Archdiocese of Denver ask enrolling families to support the Church’s teachings on sex and marriage, and they treat children according to their biological sex. Families must affirm those teachings in good faith. Colorado says those practices violate the mandate, so the parishes cannot participate. Families who want a Catholic preschool lose the benefit. Petitioners Daniel and Lisa Sheley have lost more than $12,000 so far. The lower courts largely sided with Colorado.

The free exercise clause bars the government from “prohibiting the free exercise” of religion. For decades, the court read that guarantee to require strict scrutiny of laws that substantially burden religious practice. In 1963’s Sherbert v. Verner, South Carolina denied unemployment benefits to a Seventh-day Adventist who would not work on her Sabbath. The court held that the state could not force her to choose between her faith and a public benefit without a compelling reason.

Smith changed course in 1990. Oregon had denied unemployment benefits to two men fired for using peyote in a Native American Church ceremony. Writing for the court, Justice Antonin Scalia held that a neutral law of general applicability (that is, one that neither targets religious conduct nor exempts comparable secular conduct) needs only a rational basis, however heavily it burdens religious exercise. Under that rule, the government almost always wins.

But Smith did not overrule Sherbert. It distinguished it, and the court has spent the decades since narrowing Smith’s reach. Petitioners count eight categories of free exercise cases in which the court has declined to apply it: animus toward a religious group or person (Masterpiece Cakeshop); church autonomy (Hosanna-Tabor); discrimination among religions (Larson v. Valente); forced participation in ceremonies (Barnette); hybrid rights, which pair free exercise with another constitutional right (Cantwell); parental rights over children’s religious upbringing (Mahmoud v. Taylor); penalties on religious belief as such (McDaniel v. Paty); and the receipt of public benefits (from Sherbert through Carson). Even within Smith’s domain, a law gets strict scrutiny if it is not truly “neutral” or “generally applicable,” for example because it allows individualized exemptions (Fulton) or treats comparable secular conduct more favorably (Tandon).

The public benefits category is where Carson comes in. In three cases over five years, the court held that states may not exclude religious schools from otherwise available funding. 2017’s Trinity Lutheran involved a church preschool barred from a playground-resurfacing grant. 2020’s Espinoza involved a scholarship program closed to religious schools. And in Carson, decided in 2022, Maine paid tuition at private schools but excluded schools that taught religion. The court said all of these limits violated the free exercise clause. “Regardless of how the benefit and restriction are described,” it explained, “the program operates to identify and exclude otherwise eligible schools on the basis of their religious exercise.” Its decisions, the court said, “turned on the substance of free exercise protections, not on the presence or absence of magic words.”

The Catholic preschools offer the court two routes to strict scrutiny in this case. They track the two questions the court agreed to decide.

The first route stays inside Smith. Colorado’s mandate, petitioners argue, is not generally applicable. The state lets more than 1,000 preschools limit enrollment for secular reasons but refuses to accommodate the parishes’ religious ones. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit rejected that argument, holding that a challenger must show unfettered discretion or categorical exemptions for identical secular conduct.

The second route goes around Smith. Under Carson, the preschools argue, strict scrutiny applies whenever the government conditions a generally available benefit on giving up religious exercise, whether or not the condition is neutral. Colorado, for its part, reads Carson far more narrowly, as a rule against excluding schools because they are religious. Colorado does not exclude religious preschools as such, and many participate. On that view, Carson does not apply and Smith does.

The choice between those routes is where the real stakes lie. A win on general applicability would be narrow and fragile. It would turn on the details of Colorado’s exemptions. Colorado, or any other state, could respond by trimming its secular exemptions and excluding the same schools again. The next challenger would have to start over, hunting for a new secular comparator. Principal Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Harris called that regime “an endless sort of whack-a-mole game.”

A win under Carson, in contrast, would be far more durable. It would hold that conditioning a public benefit on abandoning religious exercise triggers strict scrutiny, however the condition is drafted. That rule would stop the kind of maneuvering Maine engaged in after Carson itself, when it rewrote its program to exclude the same religious schools without using religious labels. And it would take an entire domain, public benefits, out of Smith’s reach.

That is why Thomas’ question, which this article began with, mattered. Going in, some commentators wondered whether the court would use this case to bury Smith. CNN’s Joan Biskupic framed it that way. The argument suggested something more measured, though still significant. If the court does not overrule Smith here, it seems poised to quarantine it as far as it can.

Here’s one version of what that quarantine could look like. The court can read Carson’s public benefits rule for what it says. It can apply strict scrutiny, properly understood, in that domain. It can ground that choice in the clause’s original meaning. And it can say plainly what the United States told the court: Smith is the anomaly.

Justice Neil Gorsuch asked what Colorado’s narrow reading would leave of a decade of precedent. On Colorado’s view, he wondered, had the court been “just wasting our time for the last 10 years” on Carson,Trinity Lutheran, and Espinoza? If so, any state could escape those cases by redrafting.

Indeed, states are doing exactly that. Petitioners’ counsel, Nick Reaves, told Gorsuch that “before the ink was even dry in Carson, Maine changed its laws” so that they “don’t explicitly call out religion, but they still exclude the same families and the same schools.” Colorado’s own record shows the same pattern. The state amended its discretionary enrollment exemption process during trial. More than once, it redefined an exemption that originally allowed faith-based preschools to limit enrollment to members of their congregation. Then, while the case was on appeal, it repealed that congregation exemption entirely and argued that the repeal freed it from the district court’s injunction.

Reading Carson for what it says would not create a boundless exception. Reaves located the boundary in Smith’s own concern. Smith “was concerned about every man becoming a law unto himself,” he said, and about “broad exemptions to criminal prohibitions. That interest is not as strong when it comes to public benefits when the underlying conduct is lawful.” When Justice Amy Coney Barrett asked whether a law making the mandate a condition of every preschool’s license to operate would fall under Carson, Reaves conceded, “I don’t think that would be a Carson case.”

Harris marked a second boundary. Justice Sonia Sotomayor asked about Bowen v. Roy, a 1986 decision rejecting a Native American father’s religious objection to the government’s own use of his daughter’s Social Security number. Harris pointed to the part of Bowen that commanded a majority: “You can’t force a change in the way in which the government itself manages internal operations.” Government conduct that neither pressures nor prohibits religious exercise triggers no scrutiny, as Michalyn Steele and I have explained elsewhere about Bowen. In sum, Carson’s rule has limits on both sides. It reaches conditions on public benefits for lawful conduct, not licensing regimes or the government’s management of its own affairs.

The natural worry is what comes next. If strict scrutiny governs benefits conditions, will every program become a negotiation with every objector? Justice Elena Kagan pressed this concern. Everything, she said, would turn on whether a law passes “strict scrutiny, which is a kind of balancing test, which is like how important is the state interest? How important is the religious belief? How do we compare the one to the other?”

But that is a caricature of strict scrutiny, at least as the court applies it in this context. Gorsuch offered the more accurate account, and Harris confirmed it. “[W]e assess whether the government has a compelling interest and whether it’s narrowly tailored to that interest without balancing against the interest on the other side,” Gorsuch said. Once a claimant shows a substantial burden, “[w]e don’t go balancing the two.” Gorsuch is exactly right about that.

I do not deny that older strict scrutiny opinions sometimes used the vocabulary of balancing. But the doctrine has since been disciplined, largely through the courts’ experience with the Religious Freedom Restoration Act and the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act, passed in Smith’s wake. Courts applying RFRA and RLUIPA do not ask how central a belief is to a faith. They ask a threshold question about whether the government has objectively burdened religious exercise. At the scrutiny stage, they do not weigh the value of religion against the value of a policy. As I have argued elsewhere, strict scrutiny works as an exclusionary norm paired with a heavy evidentiary burden. It excludes all but a narrow set of permissible reasons for burdening religious exercise. Then it requires the government to prove that its action is necessary to serve one of them. That’s precisely what Gorsuch described.

The court has also adopted this disciplined approach in other contexts. In United States v. Hemani last term, it held that the government cannot disarm a person merely by naming a permissible reason. It must prove that the reason is one it actually acts on, and tie that reason to the person. As I wrote at the time, history fixed the permissible ends, and the court then demanded proof that the means served them. That is how constitutional rights work more generally: as constraints on the reasons government may act on. Strict scrutiny does not ask how much religion matters. It asks whether the state’s reason is one the Constitution permits, and whether the state can prove that reason applies to this claimant.

Harris invoked Gonzales v. O Centro, the court’s leading RFRA strict scrutiny precedent, for this very point. “I think O Centro rightly recognized strict scrutiny,” she said. “[E]ven when people say it’s tough, it is a very manageable standard for courts. It’s a familiar standard for courts.” O Centro requires the government to show that its interest is served by applying the law “to the person,” meaning “the particular claimant whose sincere exercise of religion is being substantially burdened.” Courts must look “beyond broadly formulated interests” to the harm of granting the specific exemption requested.

The track record bears this out. Gorsuch noted that the federal government “already has to meet strict scrutiny” in providing its many public benefits. Harris pointed to the federal experience under RFRA and to “the 40 states that have RFRA equivalents.” Under the pre-Smith regime, she added, cases “turned out both ways.” Public schools already operate under this regime. The District of Columbia’s schools are subject to federal RFRA. As Gorsuch put it, Senators Ted Kennedy and Orrin Hatch “would be quite surprised to think that RFRA created laws unto themselves in every American.”

Smith, by contrast, is the unstable regime. The court’s cases have left what Harris called “a mess,” in which “it’s hard to describe Smith as a default, and it’s even harder to describe Smith as a workable default in this particular context.” Strict scrutiny is the familiar standard. Smith, in her words, is “a much less stable jurisprudence.”

Restoring strict scrutiny for benefits conditions would also move free exercise doctrine closer to the clause’s original meaning. Two justices asked whether strict scrutiny is faithful to that meaning, and both counsel answered yes.

Barrett asked Reaves whether strict scrutiny is “what you think is required by the original meaning.” Reaves answered that Sherbert v. Verner is “much closer to the original meaning than Smith.” He pointed to the “peace and safety provisos” in founding-era state constitutions, which protected religious exercise unless it threatened public peace or safety. Barrett then put the point precisely: “So you see it as an implementing doctrine that’s close to how it would have been implemented at the time of the founding?” “I think that’s right, yes,” Reaves said. Gorsuch asked Harris a parallel question. Is strict scrutiny, as the court announced it in Sherbert and Thomas v. Review Board and applied it in the recent benefits cases, “a reasonable construction of … the original meaning?” Harris said yes.

That framing is right. Strict scrutiny is not itself the original meaning. It is a doctrine for implementing that meaning, a form of what originalists call constitutional construction. Mark Storslee and I made this argument in our amicus brief in the case, which petitioners’ counsel also cited at argument for the history of Catholic exclusion from the common schools. The brief draws on my work elsewhere, including Constructing Constitutional Rights and Replacing Smith.

The core of the argument is this. The founding generation did not let religious exercise yield to any reason government happened to articulate. Early state constitutions took some justifications for burdening religious exercise off the table. Others, most commonly the protection of public peace and safety, were permissible. And founding-era courts made the government show that it was actually advancing one of those permissible interests before religious exercise had to give way. For example, in People v. Philips, decided in 1813, a New York court refused to force a Catholic priest to testify about a confession. Compelling him, the court explained, would place him “between Scylla and Charybdis,” and the priest’s silence posed no threat to the peace or safety the state constitution protected. That is what strict scrutiny requires: a permissible reason, proven on the facts.

The evidence from Reconstruction points the same way. The 14th Amendment, which applies the free exercise clause to the states, was framed by a generation shaped by religious resistance to the Fugitive Slave Act. Abolitionist believers insisted on a right to give a fugitive shelter and a “crust of bread,” whatever neutral and generally applicable law said. As Kurt Lash and I have explained, that understanding informed the amendment’s privileges or immunities clause. Judge Ryan Nelson of the 9th Circuit relied on that history in a recent concurrence concluding that Smith “breaks from the history and tradition surrounding free exercise and the Fourteenth Amendment.” At argument, Harris agreed with Justice Brett Kavanaugh that, as a matter of original meaning and contrary to Smith, the free exercise clause is “more than simply a protection against explicit discrimination.”

One serious question about the Carson approach came from Kavanaugh. A rule that applies strict scrutiny to benefits conditions, but not to outright bans, would impose “greater First Amendment scrutiny on a benefits program than … an outright ban on the religious conduct.” That, he said, “seems inverted.” On petitioners’ theory, a state that merely withholds funding would face strict scrutiny, while a state that banned the same conduct outright, through a neutral law, would get only Smith’s rational basis review. He acknowledged one answer, that the court “should just overrule Smith entirely,” but asked Reaves to assume that was off the table.

The incoherence is real. And if the court doesn’t overrule Smith in this case, hopefully it will take that step someday soon. But the incoherence belongs to Smith itself. Harris put it directly: “Smith is the anomaly in the context of public benefits or in any other context, where other rights do not have this so long as a law is generally applicable rational basis review.”

Smith itself claimed the opposite, calling religious exemptions “a constitutional anomaly.” As Mark Rienzi and I have argued, the reverse is true. Exemptions are a species of as-applied challenge, the default remedy elsewhere in constitutional law. The anomaly is Smith’s rule, not the exemptions it disfavors.

The court has retired other precedents it no longer believes in. It distinguishes them, whittles them away, and finally overrules them. Teague v. Lane’s “watershed” exception for new rules of criminal procedure went unused for 32 years before Edwards v. Vannoy declared it “moribund” and eliminated it. Gorsuch joined that opinion. Abood v. Detroit Board of Education was cabined inHarris v. Quinn before Janus v. AFSCME overruled it. Lemon v. Kurtzman was sidestepped for years before Kennedy v. Bremerton confirmed that the court had “long ago abandoned” it.

After decades of whittling, quarantine is the penultimate stage of that life cycle. The court can further limit Smith’s damage now. Eventually the court will likely complete the life cycle and retire Smith altogether.

The most striking moments in the argument were strict scrutiny questions in all but name. Justice Samuel Alito asked how many times the feared harm had actually happened, and observed that there was “little evidence of a practical problem.” Barrett asked whether there was any record of LGBTQ parents being turned away from these preschools, and whether any entity other than religious ones had sought an exemption from the mandate. “No, Your Honor,” Colorado’s counsel answered. Kavanaugh asked the state, “Why not seek the win/win?” With roughly 2,000 preschools in the program and 34 Catholic ones, he saw “plenty of opportunities to respect the rights of the religious believers and respect the ability of LGBT parents to find” a school that fits. “Why has this been provoked?” he asked.

Those are the questions narrow tailoring forces a government to answer. Strict scrutiny asks whether the state can prove that its reason applies here, not merely name it. That demand makes room for the win-win Kavanaugh described. Religious preschools can serve the families who want them, and every family can find a school that fits. Smith invites the opposite: winner-take-all conflicts provoked by a rule that never asks whether the conflict was necessary.

The best case for quarantining Smith is not that religious claimants deserve to win. It is that strict scrutiny asks the questions this argument kept asking: Why are we here, and couldn’t we have avoided this conflict? A rule that makes the government answer those questions is easy to administer. It is also faithful to the clause’s original meaning.

Disclosure: The author was amicus curiae in support of the petitioners in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy.

Stephanie Barclay is a Professor of Law at Georgetown Law School, and the Faculty Director of the Georgetown Center for the Constitution.

Recommended Citation: Stephanie Barclay, St. Mary and the shrinking reach of Smith, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 5, 2026, 10:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/st-mary-and-the-shrinking-reach-of-smith/

#7570. Ninth Circuit curtails California greenhouse gas disclosure laws

The appellate court agreed with the U.S. Chamber of Commerce that the laws in part amounted to compelled speech that wasn't merited by California's interest in reducing emissions.

(CN) â The Ninth Circuit said Monday that two California laws that require large corporations to disclose their greenhouse gas emissions and report their climate-related financial risk are either in part or completely unconstitutional.

In a split decision, the panel affirmed in part and reversed in part a decision by a trial judge last year who rejected the U.S. Chamber of Commerce’s bid to halt enforcement of the two state laws until their constitutionality was decided.

The panel said California’s Climate-Related Financial Risk Act, also known as SB 261, runs afoul of First Amendment protections against compelled speech because the required disclosures were akin to “subjective ideological assessments” rather than commercial speech, such as warning labels, that don’t require strict scrutiny to decide if a law infringes on a constitutional right.

“SB 261 requires companies to opine on whether climate change poses financial risks to their operations and business model, thereby making predictive judgments about uncertain future conditions,” U.S. Circuit Judge Jacqueline Nguyen wrote.

“The compelled disclosures require companies to go beyond providing economic information tethered to any commercial transaction,” the Barack Obama appointee added. “Instead, companies must share value-laden judgments on a politically fraught subject, and thus the disclosures fall outside the commercial speech doctrine.”

Given that it doesn’t regulate commercial speech, SB 261 fails strict scrutiny because it isn’t narrowly tailored enough to meet California’s purported interest in “mitigating information asymmetries for investors, reducing emissions and correcting misleading speech,” Nguyen said.

The second law the U.S. Chamber of Commerce challenged is the Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act, SB 253, which requires corporations with over $1 billion in annual revenue that operate in California to report greenhouse gas emissions from sources they directly own or control, the emissions from the companiesâ purchased energy and the indirect emissions from their value chain, including those from their suppliers and customers.

The majority agreed the first two requirements regulate commercial speech because they compel disclosure of factual information on emissions generated through the reporting entitiesâ own operations and bear on capital transactions.

Moreover, California has demonstrated substantial interests in mitigating information asymmetries for investors and reducing emissions, as well as a likelihood these two disclosure requirements directly advance its interests and are no more extensive than necessary, the panel said.

The appellate court upheld the trial judge’s denial of a preliminary injunction for those two requirements.

As for the third requirement, insofar as it concerns diffuse third-party conduct in the value chain, it is insufficientlylinked to a company’s own operations and capital transactions to qualify as commercial speech, the panel said and reversed the judge’s denial of a preliminary injunction for that part of SB 253.

In November, the Ninth Circuit panel had already stayed enforcement of SB 261 pending appeal, but it declined to do so for SB 253. Part of the latter law went into effect last month.

U.S. Circuit Judge Mark Bennett dissented and wrote the majority equated investorsâ interest in companies with consumersâ interest in products by finding the two requirements of SB 253 passed intermediate scrutiny insofar as they address California’s interest in mitigating information asymmetries for investors.

This, the Donald Trump appointee said, could open the door to states requiring companies to disclose a host of otherwise unavailable information to address information asymmetries that might be useful to investors, such as, for example, the number of undocumented immigrant workers at a company.

Senior U.S. District Judge Kiyo Matsumoto, a George W. Bush appointee at the U.S. District Court in Brooklyn, New York, who was sitting by designation, rounded out the panel.

âTheÂ Ninth Circuitâs decisionÂ toÂ haltÂ the most onerous parts ofÂ CaliforniaâsÂ climate disclosure lawsÂ is an important victoryÂ for businessesÂ andÂ the protection of their First Amendment rights," Daryl Joseffer, Â president of the U.S. Chamber Litigation Center, said in a statement.Â “TheÂ injunction prevents the state from imposing massive compliance costs on companies,Â especially small businesses, andÂ confirms thatÂ states cannotÂ unilaterallyÂ impose sweeping, extraterritorial mandates.â

In a statement to Courthouse News, California Attorney General’s Office representatives said they âare pleased that reporting under SB 253 will move forward, providing valuable Scope 1 and Scope 2 information to California stakeholders. We are evaluating next steps and remain committed to protecting Californiansâ access to critical climate data in a changing world.â

David Duongâs attorney, Edward Swanson, pointed out discrepancies between how much Juarez expensed the Duongs for several flights between Oakland and San Diego â the modular home construction facility was in Mexico â and how much the flights cost, according to Juarezâs bank statements subpoenaed directly from Chase Bank.

Swanson also asked Juarez if he became an informant because he wanted to get back at the Duongs for the failure of Evolutionary Homes and after the purported bribes to Thao and Jones failed to materialize with real contracts.

âYou wanted to hurt them?â asked Swanson.

âHurting CWS is not the purpose,â answered Juarez, referring to California Waste Solutions.

Swanson then showed a text message Juarez sent to Andreas Cluver, the vice president at the Port of Oakland, two days before meeting with prosecutors.

U.S. Assistant Attorney Abraham Fine objected to the text as hearsay but was overruled by Rogers.

On cross-examination, Shawn Halbert, Jonesâ attorney, asked why, if Evolutionary Homes was so important to Juarez, would he immediately turn to bribing public officials to get it off the ground.

At one point, Juarez also admitted that he talked to witnesses about their previous testimony regarding the mailers and read newspaper accounts of what was said during the trial, behavior against the rules of the court.

The trial, and Juarez’s cross-examination, continues Tuesday.

#7566. Court leans toward narrow ruling on inmate’s use of habeas for accelerated transfer to a halfway house or home confinement

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court heard oral argument on Nov. 2 in Maxwell v. Dinis about whether a federal inmate may use a habeas statute, 28 U.S.C. § 2241, to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement.

Maxwell, a former attorney, was convicted at trial for his role in conspiring with a mob-related organization, La Costa Nostra, to take over a Texas-based mortgage-loan company, FirstPlus Financial Group, Inc., and drain it of its assets. As Maxwell neared the end of his sentence, he sought to contest the BOP’s calculation of good-time credits that would accelerate his transfer from prison to a halfway house or home confinement. The question for the court was whether Section 2241, which does not clearly spell out what claims may be brought but whose scope has largely been shaped by precedent, allows him to do so.

Maxwell’s attorney, Masha Hansford, pressed for a broad rule that habeas is available to an inmate like Maxwell who is asserting a right to a “distinct and lower level of custody.” But that position almost immediately encountered some pushback. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson questioned “whether we really need to use this case to define every circumstance in which habeas is appropriate.” Hansford agreed that the court need not adopt a test that allows inmates to challenge all changes to the level of custody and was content to have the court resolve Maxwell’s case by applying a narrower test endorsed by the government that would permit an inmate to use habeas to challenge the denial of an accelerated transfer to parole or, as here, a halfway house or home confinement.

Justice Samuel Alito pressed Hansford on whether an inmate may use Section 2241 simply to dispute how BOP calculated good-time credits or whether the inmate must also show that any error in calculating would also entitle the inmate to accelerated transfer to a halfway house or home confinement. After Hansford replied that Maxwell met all the requirements for the transfer and only the calculation of good-time credits was at issue, Justice Neal Gorsuch followed up by pressing whether the court needs to say that an inmate could bring a habeas challenge about the calculation of good-time credits alone. Hansford replied that the court did not need to say a dispute over good-time credits alone would suffice for a federal inmate to bring a claim in Section 2241.

Turning to Hansford’s level-of-custody test, Justice Sonia Sotomayor noted that, in a prior case, Justice Antonin Scalia had referred to habeas as covering a “‘quantum change’ in the level of custody,” but Hansford was asking the court “to create new language, ‘materially less restrictive custody.’ Why don’t we stick to what we have?” Hansford agreed that the court need not broaden its test and that Maxwell’s requested transfer to a halfway house or home confinement amounted to such a quantum change.

Assistant to the Solicitor General Kevin J. Barber, arguing for the government, contended that “there’s no need to adopt” Maxwell’s “amorphous level-of-custody rule.” He explained that the court “has always made clear that habeas is available when your claim is seeking discharge from actual physical confinement in prison to a different kind of custody,” such as a halfway house or home confinement. Here, the government relied heavily on Preiser v. Rodriguez, which held that habeas supplies the sole avenue for a state inmate to challenge the denial of credit toward release on parole.

When Gorsuch pressed Barber on the source of the government’s rule and why an inmate’s transfer to solitary confinement or maximum security would not be covered, Barber pointed principally to history and tradition in the court’s habeas cases. Barber explained, “we don’t have any tradition of claims being recognized as habeas claims challenging just transfers within prison systems.”

Despite agreeing that Maxwell could bring his claim in Section 2241, the government argued that no court could actually grant him relief. Specifically, the government pointed to 18 U.S.C. § 3621(b) and its terms barring courts from reviewing “a designation of a place of imprisonment under this subsection.” According to the government, service of a sentence in a halfway house or home confinement is “a designation of a place of imprisonment” governed by that statute.

But the government did not appear to have the votes to prevail on this argument, at least at the Supreme Court. Justice Brett Kavanaugh pressed Barber on whether that issue could be left for the lower court to decide on remand. Barber conceded that the court “absolutely could.” Sotomayor questioned Barber about whether the government is right that Section 3621(b) applies to Maxwell’s claim. But after Barber began responding, Justice Amy Coney Barrett reiterated Kavanaugh’s point that “we don’t have to get into any of this, right?” Barber again agreed.

Jackson pressed Barber on a separate point, that the BOP is expected to transfer Maxwell to a halfway house or home confinement in January 2027, which would soon make his claim moot. Jackson disputed why the court would revisit its decision to hear the case. Barber apologized for not pressing the Section 3621(b) issue or mootness in opposing certiorari, but said these factors spoke in favor of the court dismissing the case as improvidently granted.

The amicus, Brian W. Barnes, was appointed to argue in favor of the ruling by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit that habeas is unavailable for Maxwell’s claim. When pressed by Justice Elena Kagan, Barnes agreed that habeas is available to “encompass a move from incarceration to parole,” as Preiser held. Kagan pointed out that “parole looks an awful lot like what’s going on here.”

The justices’ questions suggest that they are unlikely to limit Preiser and reject an analogy between Maxwell’s requested relief and the parole in that case. The justices also showed little appetite for reaching the government’s Section 3621(b) argument. How they would handle Maxwell’s expected release to a halfway house in January 2027 was less clear, but that circumstance could result in a speedier ruling.

Richard D. Cooke worked for the U.S. Department of Justice for 23 years, first at the Antitrust Division for 5 years and then as an Assistant United States Attorney in the Eastern District of Virginia for 18 years.
